news.title: Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges
news.text: President Donald Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi, as he continued a closing midterm rally blitz that has highlighted Republicans' challenges ahead of an election that could drastically shift power in Washington and statehouses across the country.“I'm here because Cindy’s doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can’t take a chance,” Trump told the crowd, his voice audibly hoarse, as he worked to boost Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who is facing a surprisingly stiff challenge from Democrat Scott Colom.Colom was spotted at the rally site, too, creating the rare spectacle of Trump's staunchest supporters interacting directly with a figure the president would soon go on to denigrate as a “Marxist radical” and “fake" and “shameless phony who pretends to be a moderate” from the stage.Mississippi, among the nation’s most reliably Republican states, is not where the GOP envisioned needing a late-October stop from the president. But Colom is one of many Democratic underdogs who have managed to expand the House and Senate battleground maps because of widespread voter discontent over inflation, the Iran war and other aspects of Trump’s second presidency.He said he had planned to go to the rally site to listen to what was on Trump supporters' minds."They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said ahead of the president's arrival.Trump's event kicks off a week of aggressive campaigning that will include more stops in states he won comfortably in 2024, including Texas, South Carolina and Iowa.RELATED STORY | Trump heads to Mississippi as more red states enter the midterm conversation with 8 days to goDemocrats, including progressives, are expanding their effortsTop Democratic candidates and their surrogates were also greeting voters — more than 30 million of whom have already cast ballots, according to data collected by The Associated Press from election administrators across the country — as they try to end Republicans' threadbare majority in the House, take over a Senate majority that was once thought secure for Republicans and end the GOP’s national advantage in state capitals.Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats' 2024 presidential candidate, campaigned in Wisconsin with Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who faces Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Trump ally, for governor. Crowley would be the state’s first Black governor if elected to lead the battleground state.“This is a tight race because the stakes are so high,” Harris said at the event billed as a “Women for Crowley” rally.Meanwhile, in Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced himself from an ad created by a political action committee called Rebellion PAC that blames high grocery prices on U.S. support for Israel.“This ad is not affiliated in any way with the Abdul for Senate campaign,” a spokesperson for El-Sayed, Roxie Richner, said in a statement about the spot, which features a couple discussing U.S. support for Israel as they shop for groceries.“Apparently it’s costing us a lot of money to drop bombs on Gaza,” the woman says.The ad had been condemned by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic primary.The way to win Michigan “is not by blaming the high costs of our goods on the only Jewish homeland in the world,” Stevens wrote on X.El-Sayed, who would be the country’s first Muslim senator, has denounced antisemitism while fiercely criticizing Israel for its military operations in Gaza — a position that has been a frequent point of attack for both Republicans and supporters of Israel in his party.Vance campaigning in other Republican statesVice President JD Vance traveled to Kansas to stump for Sen. Roger Marshall, who finds himself in a tight contest with Democratic nominee and pastor Adam Hamilton. Hundreds of people were gathered inside the warehouse of a steel-fabricating company in north Topeka in a state where Democrats haven’t won a Senate race since 1932.Marshall told the crowd that Trump is on the ballot, even if his name doesn’t appear, because of how Democrats will thwart his agenda if they win control of Congress.“Democrats are coming out like it’s a presidential year,” he said, calling on the GOP to match Democrats’ energy.Jace Sullivan, a 50-year-old electrician from Topeka who describes himself as “85% Republican,” said Trump supporters need to “circle the wagons” and get out to vote.Wearing a red “JD Vance for President 2028" shirt, he said he thinks Trump is rightly working to keep Iran from getting nuclear weapons.“Gas prices are high and it does suck, but it’s a means to an end,” Sullivan said.Trump, at the Mississippi rally, said he had, in fact, expected gas prices to rise even higher than they had.“It worked out fine and it’ll be over soon,” he said of the war with Iran.Earlier, Vance was in Belgrade, Montana, to campaign with Republican Aaron Flint, who is facing Democrat Sam Forstag in the race for the state’s 1st Congressional District, and Republican Senate candidate Kurt Alme.Sen. Tim Scott, who serves as chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told The Associated Press Monday that GOP candidates are “closing very strongly” in races across the country, including South Carolina, which Trump is set to visit for the second time in as many weeks to stump for GOP Sen. Darline Graham.“One of the reasons why we will be in the majority is because he has invested the time and the energy on the campaign trail,” Scott said on the sidelines of U.S. Rep. Russell Fry’s 3rd Annual Freedom Fry event.RELATED STORY | Democrats fear slippage with Black voters makes Michigan Senate race feel ‘far closer than it should’Trump to rally in another reliably Republican stateBut it's Trump's visit to Mississippi that perhaps brings the midterm landscape into the sharpest relief with just a week of campaigning left.To be sure, Hyde-Smith, who is vying for her second full term, remains the favorite in a state Trump won three times by an average of nearly 20 percentage points.But Colom, a local prosecutor who would make history as Mississippi's first Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction, is looking to parlay inflation, Trump's lagging popularity and Hyde-Smith's mistakes into an upset.Senate Democrats’ super PAC has been a late entry in the contest, with a $1.2 million investment. Mississippians have not chosen a new Democratic senator since 1947, and Democrats last won a Senate race there when that senator, the onetime segregationist John Stennis, won his last reelection in 1982.In New York, meanwhile, one of the party’s most vulnerable House members pulled from Trump’s campaign playbook. Rep. Mike Lawler, who is in a tight race with Democrat Cait Conley in New York City’s northern suburbs, manned a McDonald’s drive-thru — mimicking something Trump did two years ago, even as Lawler has tried to emphasize his independence from the president.
news.summary: President Donald Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi, as he continued a closing midterm rally blitz.

news.title: Former VP Kamala Harris campaigns for David Crowley in Milwaukee
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris joined Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley to rally a crowd of about 450 supporters on Oct. 26 at the Pfister Hotel in downtown Milwaukee.

"This is an extraordinary state that means so much to so many people," Harris said. "And you – the leaders in the room – mean everything in terms of what we are fighting for, what we care about, and who we are as Americans."

The event, dubbed Women for Crowley, came just over a week before Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, and his opponent, Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, face off in the Nov. 3 election.

Harris slammed Tiffany as an election denier before laying into Republican President Donald Trump and his administration.

"Let's talk about what is important about this moment in our country, where we are seeing such brutality come out of the highest office in the land," she said. "Where we are seeing the corruption of well... the most callous and corrupt and incompetent presidential administration in the history of America."

But she urged the crowd to turn their frustration into action.

"I see you, and you matter, and your voice matters," Harris said. "And you don't have to put up with this stuff."

Harris spoke last, after Crowley and his wife, Ericka, spoke of their frustration with high gas and grocery prices throughout Wisconsin and across the country.

Ericka described her husband as "a man who understands the struggle," adding that his family had been evicted three times before graduating from high school. She also took aim at Tiffany's comments during last week's debate encouraging Wisconsin women to trust him.

"We don't trust you, Tom," she said to applause, noting that he had supported federal legislation that would have restricted access to six weeks of pregnancy − before many women know they are pregnant. His position previously raised concerns among Republicans ahead of his entrance to the governor's race.

David Crowley also repeatedly linked Tiffany to Trump, saying Tiffany "went to Washington, D.C., and sold Wisconsin out."

"He went to go work for the billionaires who are bankrolling his campaign," he said.

Tiffany pushed back in a statement, saying, "David Crowley wants to bring Kamala Harris’ California playbook to Wisconsin, and all you have to do is look at his record to know it's true."

He criticized Crowley's record on issues like taxes and immigration, and criticized campaign money that the Democratic Party of Wisconsin has received from billionaire Reid Hoffman, whose name appeared hundreds of times in the Epstein files.

"Wisconsin rejected Kamala Harris once, and now it’s time to reject David Crowley," Tiffany said.

Early voting still underway, lagging numbers in Milwaukee County

Early voting has been underway for one week in Wisconsin and runs through Nov. 1, though locations and hours vary by community.

In Milwaukee County, 70,033 voters have already cast ballots as of Oct. 26 at in-person early voting sites or by returning mail-in ballots.

That's slightly down from the last midterm election in 2022 featuring a governor's race, when 72,381 Milwaukee County voters had voted early eight days out from Election Day. Clerks have said Wisconsin might see a decrease in mail-in voting, and a boost in voting at polling places on Election Day, because of continued concerns over mail delays.

Sherlyn Ramirez, 20, was attending the rally and said she had voted early.

"But I still wanted to come out and be a part of the community," said Ramirez, who attended the event with her younger sister. Both were wearing Brewers gear and planned to watch the World Series game set to start one hour after the event got underway.

At one point during Harris' remarks, a supporter shouted "Go Brewers!" Harris, a San Francisco Giants supporter, wished Milwaukee luck but joked, "I'm not touching that."

Ramirez said she was especially concerned with issues like immigration and voting rights.

"I know there's been a lot of debate, but there's never going to be a perfect candidate, but we have to stick together," Ramirez said, noting she attended the 2024 Harris rally in West Allis. "I'm nervous, but I'm hopeful."

Melinda Cunningham-St. Clair, who lives in Racine and works at Mount Mary University as an adjunct facilitator, said she votes early in-person and that her husband had already mailed in his ballot.

"I now vote early, hopefully for calmer crowds," she said. "It's not as tense when I walk in, and I appreciate that."

Asked how she was feeling about the upcoming election, Cunningham-St. Clair said she was "a little reluctant, hesitant – hopeful based on some of the turnout I see here."

"But it's a very unstable political climate still, and so I think we still feel that," she added.

The latest poll from Marquette University Law School had Crowley at a slight advantage over Tiffany. The final Marquette poll before the Nov. 3 election is set to be released Oct. 28.

Democratic presidential contenders in Wisconsin, but no Trump visit yet

Harris' trip to Wisconsin is her latest stop on the campaign trail in the leadup to the midterms as she tries to help Democrats in tight races – and weighs a 2028 run for president.

Another presidential contender, former Biden Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, is also scheduled to campaign with Crowley Nov. 2. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, another possible 2028 candidate, appeared with Crowley earlier this month.

This isn't the first time Crowley and Harris have appeared together during his run for governor. Crowley previously attended a fundraiser with Harris and actor Sean Penn in California last month.

In a statement, Republican Governors Association communications director Kollin Crompton said Harris and Crowley "are both soft-on-crime, tax hiking liberals."

"Just add this to the list of terrible decisions David Crowley has made in his career," Crompton said.

More: Sheriff's office follows Crowley's lead, suspends tablet messaging at county jail

After stumping for Crowley at the Pfister, Harris was set to headline a second Milwaukee event with NAACP President and CEO Derrick Johnson. Crowley was not scheduled to appear at the town-hall style event.

The event was hosted at St. Mark AME Church, founded more than a century ago by Ezekiel Gillespie, who fought and successfully sued for Black men's right to vote in Wisconsin. Considered the first Black church in Milwaukee, St. Mark has recently received historical recognition, including an honorary street sign for the late Rev. Dr. Lovell Johnson Sr.

Harris will headline a similar event with the NAACP in Georgia Oct. 29.

Earlier this month, former President Barack Obama, the first Black president, endorsed Crowley in a video posted Oct. 8. In it, Obama – who won Wisconsin twice – compared Crowley's background to his own. If elected, Crowley would be Wisconsin's first Black governor.

President Donald Trump has also waded into Wisconsin's governor race, announcing in January that he was endorsing Tiffany. Most recently, Trump hinted at a potential Wisconsin visit in a Truth Social post on Oct. 7.

Trump has been traveling around the country on campaign visits, most recently in Michigan, but has not yet announced plans to return to Wisconsin. The president was last in the state in June when he spoke at a farm in Chippewa Falls. Members of his administration have joined U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden in his competitive race.

More: Trump dangles a Wisconsin trip as some in GOP back away

Trump won Wisconsin in 2016 and 2024 but lost in 2020. Harris' visit comes amid speculation about her potential 2028 presidential bid, which she hasn't publicly ruled out. In 2024, Harris lost Wisconsin to Trump by under one percentage point.

Hope Karnopp can be reached at HKarnopp@usatodayco.com.

news.title: Don’t trust the polls: Make YOUR poll count – and vote!
news.text:
To vote or not to vote. That is the question. Are you serious? Can any conscientious Christians sit this one out? But apparently, there are some who may just do that, for whatever reason.

The only poll that counts is the vote that you cast.

Are we seeing the left’s attempt to suppress the conservative vote? It’s all over. Why bother anymore?

An article by M.D. Kittle in the Federalist.com caught my eye: “‘Absolute scumbags.’ That’s how Democrat strategist and former Kamala Harris adviser Mike Nellis described Wedgewood Polling, another faux ‘election survey company’ confessing that it made up numbers. Why? Wedgewood claims their bogus polls – rolled out in two widely watched Democratic Party primaries – were just an ‘experimental project.'” [emphasis added]

Just an “experiment”? But some people may have decided to sit this one out because of same.

Meanwhile, even if the polls favoring abortion and the transgender agenda and open border type policies were correct, it would still behoove the Bible-based Christian to vote and to vote their biblical values, to not be fooled by those who also claim to believe in the Bible and yet take positions in opposition to the plain teaching of Scripture. This includes Texas U.S. senatorial candidate James Talarico, whose radical views I have commented on elsewhere.

Rev. Franklin Graham warns that Christians should not sit out the 2026 midterms: “The choice is yours, but look prayerfully at what both parties stand for.”

The late Dr. D. James Kennedy once declared that it’s a sin not to vote. His proof-text was from the passage in the Gospels, where Jesus said that we should render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and unto God the things that are God’s (Mark 12:17).

Historically, Christians in America applied their faith to virtually every sphere of life, including their politics. While the Founding Fathers were not all Christians, the vast majority of them were, and more importantly they had a biblical worldview.

Samuel Adams, the spark plug of the whole push for American independence (without whom there likely would not have been America at 250), once said this on the importance of voting: “Let each citizen remember at the moment he is offering his vote … that he is executing one of the most solemn trusts in human society for which he is accountable to God and his country.”

When we vote biblical values, we obey what the Lord would have us do. Jesus is not on the ballot, so ultimately we are voting for a sinner. But the question is where does that sinner stand on key issues?

Where do they stand on abortion? We know that many women today have been deceived into aborting their child, thinking that would simply end their problem. In reality, it has created many more problems. But there’s forgiveness and healing through Christ.

Where do the politicians stand on religious liberty? We know that many, if not most, of those who initially settled America came here for religious liberty. Today, that freedom is in jeopardy.

What types of judges will these politicians give us? Those that promote sin or those that would uphold justice?

The Bible declares that righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people (Proverbs 14:34).

There are some Christians who are so upset with the high price of gas because of the Iranian conflict that they will sit this election out. But their non-vote is a vote – a vote for someone with whom they probably would disagree vehemently.

For this column, I reached out to Dr. Alveda King, the niece of Martin Luther King Jr., asking her for any charge to the faithful. Evangelist King is the founder and director of Speak for Life.

Alveda told me: “Don’t let a poll or a headline talk you out of voting. Polls don’t cast ballots. People do. God made us of one blood, one human family, and we have a responsibility to care for our neighbors and the generations coming behind us. Pray for wisdom. Examine the candidates and their policies. Vote your faith, not your fear. Let your convictions guide your choices, and treat those who disagree with dignity. Whatever the predictions say, do your part. Don’t surrender your voice before you have used it.” Amen.

For a radio segment, I interviewed Debbie Wuthnow of ivoterguide.com about the midterms. She told our listeners: “100% we need to vote. God commanded us to be salt and light and we need to be salt and light in that government.”

It is a privilege to vote. It is our Christian duty to vote. So, vote your biblical values. If enough Christians show up and vote biblical values, we could carry this election – and every election.
news.summary: 'Whatever the predictions say, do your part. Don't surrender your voice before you have used it'
news.author: Jerry Newcombe

news.title: Democrats, polls paint a picture of election manipulation
news.text:
With the midterm election looming on Nov. 3, Democrats are determined to dismantle any election safeguards aimed at preventing non-citizens from voting.

This includes making sure that voter registration rolls stay dirty.

On Oct. 20, Democratic congressional leaders and several Democratic groups filed a federal lawsuit against the Department of Homeland Security for its directive to states to clean up their voter rolls by removing non-citizens.

Democrats oppose cooperation between state officials and federal officials to share databases to ensure that voter eligibility is limited to U.S. citizens.

They argue that it’s a matter of states’ rights. This, from a party that now embraces socialism and has treated the states like vassals under the federal government.

The Constitution designates the states to determine when and where to hold elections, but it does not preclude the federal government from making sure that only U.S. citizens 18 and over can vote in federal elections.

Officials in Arlington County, Virginia, a Democratic stronghold, also filed a lawsuit in federal court against the U.S. Justice Department and other agencies. Their goal is to bar federal agents from coming anywhere near polling places, even to collar illegal alien criminals.

The plaintiffs claim that voters would be intimidated if they spot immigration authorities. Well, certainly anyone ineligible to vote might think twice about doing so upon seeing ICE agents outside the polls. Maybe that’s not such a bad idea.

The lawsuit was filed with the help of two left-wing foundations – Democracy Forward and the Public Rights Project. Both are funded by leftist philanthropy groups, including the Tides network, which is funded by the George Soros family’s Open Society Foundation.

Democracy Forward is chaired by Marc Elias. He was general counsel for Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign, and his law firm secured the fraudulent Steele dossier, which was used in the Russian collusion hoax against President Donald Trump.

Mr. Elias has played a major role in the Democrats’ ongoing campaign to weaken or overturn election integrity laws wherever they can. So, it’s no wonder that his Democracy Forward is working to ensure that non-citizens feel comfortable going to the polls.

Democrats are also sowing distrust about the validity of the election in case it goes against them.

The Washington Post on Wednesday ran a front-page story alleging that a group of “U.S. national security officials” has been advising state lawmakers that the Trump administration may try to interfere with the midterms.

Democratic strategy appears to be three-fold:

Sow doubts about the election in case Republicans win.

Accuse anyone asking questions about election integrity in Democratic-run jurisdictions to be part of a Trump plan to subvert the process.

Keep repeating the old chestnut about voter ID laws “suppressing the minority vote.” Democrats insist that minorities can’t be expected to have valid IDs like other citizens.

Current polls show a Democratic tide. If the GOP manages to hold the Congress, Democrats will cry foul and somehow blame Mr. Trump for skullduggery.

The Post ran its own survey, along with ABC News and Ipso, and published an article on Wednesday with this headline: “Most Americans doubt Trump would accept GOP losses.”

The poll says that 77 percent of independents and 94 percent of Democrats said they were not confident that Mr. Trump “would accept GOP losses.”

That’s a one-two punch: the scary story with anonymous sources on the front page and the poll just inside.

Speaking of polls, you probably have heard about the Wedgewood Polling scandal. A fake company by that name showed Democrats ahead in key races. Several media outlets took the bait, including the New York Times, MS Now and The Hill.

On Oct. 20, Wedgewood admitted to faking the data after it was outed by polling aggregator FiftyPlusOne. As of this past week, we had yet to learn who funded it.

Wedgewood Polling “gave Democrats multipoint leads beginning in June in all the battleground races: Texas, Michigan, Georgia, Maine, Ohio and Kansas,” according to the Washington Times’ Susan Ferrachio and George Caldwell.

It even made the U.S. Senate race a “toss up” in staunchly GOP Mississippi, which the nonpartisan Cook Political Report says is “Likely Republican.”

Polls can affect outcomes. Voters who think their candidate has no chance might sit it out or cast a ballot for someone else. In the Michigan U.S. Senate primary in June, Wedgewood said Democrat Mallory McMorrow’s support had collapsed to less than 10%. She blames this partly for her loss.

Abdul El-Sayed, the winner, is shown by most polls to be leading Republican Rep. Mike Rogers.

Or maybe he isn’t.

In 2024, three days before the Nov. 5 election, the final Selzer/Des Moines Register poll showed Democrat Kamala Harris leading Donald Trump by 47 percent to 44 percent among likely Iowa voters. Mr. Trump wound up winning by 13 points, a 16-point discrepancy.

At the time, most media reported the poll, which was real, with some at least noting that it differed from other Iowa surveys.

Joe Scarborough of MSNBC’s “Morning Joe,” however, trumpeted it as “a canary in the coal mine.”

It’s this kind of stuff that podcaster Stephen Miller calls “leftist media wish-casting.”

This column was first published at the Washington Times.
news.summary: 'Voters who think their candidate has no chance might sit it out or cast a ballot for someone else'

news.title: “Prediction” Markets Were Comically Wrong About the Brazilian Election
news.text:
Down in Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff election on Sunday to be re-elected as president, in a comeback that literally defied the odds — at least as they’d been set by buzzy prediction markets.

Though platforms like Polymarket frame themselves as prognosticators of the future by drawing on the “wisdom of the crowd,” they were horrendously off the mark when it came to Brazil’s extremely consequential election. 

After the first round of voting on October 4, the Polymarket odds that Flávio Bolsonaro — the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27 year sentence for leading a coup attempt — would win the election surged to over 80 percent, while Luna’s chances of winning bottomed out at a dismal 12 percent.

The extremely favorable odds for Bolsonaro held for over a week — up until the very day that the second round of voting was held. That Sunday morning, Polymarket odds showed Bolsonaro having an 81 percent chance of winning.

What actually happened was a staggering upset, if you based your expectations for the future on a glorified gambling platform. Lula defeated Bolsonaro by 51.8 percent to 48.2 percent, according to official election results, in a huge rebuff to a mounting right-wing wave in Latin America.

Over $62 million in bets were placed on Bolsonaro winning the election. But his odds quickly collapsed to as low 15 percent as the day went on and early polls trickled out, causing more bets to pour in in favor of Lula. 

Of course, a one-off upset doesn’t in itself meaning that prediction markets don’t provide some insight, just as a clear day when the forecast showed an 80 percent rain doesn’t mean meteorologists don’t know what they’re doing.

But actual on-the-ground polling showed that the election would be a tight race, while Polymarket’s vaunted “prediction data” had Bolsonaro as an overwhelming favorite. Recall that when Polymarket successfully predicted a decisive Donald Trump victory over Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, it was touted as a major coup over traditional polling that had the race as a toss-up. It’s only fair then that when Polymarket gets a major election so drastically wrong, it should also reflect on its credibility — negatively.

The usefulness of prediction markets as a barometer of public sentiment, if not an actual means of feeling out the future, is still unclear, despite what companies running them might claim. They remain hotbeds of insider trading, while massive wagers placed by a handful of wealthy bettors can distort odds and overpower the proverbial wisdom of the majority of the crowd.

Stateside, their credibility will face another major test during the upcoming midterm elections in November.

More on prediction markets: Senator Who Tried to Ban Prediction Markets Gets Hired by Kalshi as a Lobbyist
news.summary:
Flávio Bolsonaro was the overwhelming favorite, right up until the moment he unceremoniously lost.

news.title: Trump heads to Mississippi for a midterm rally, and the Democrat he wants defeated is going, too
news.text:
CORINTH, Miss. (AP) — President Donald Trump heads Monday to Mississippi, as he continues a closing midterm campaign blitz that highlights Republicans’ challenges ahead of an election that could drastically shift power in Washington and statehouses across the country.

The Democratic Senate candidate Trump wants to help defeat, Scott Colom, said he’s going to the president’s rally site, too — creating the rare spectacle of Trump’s staunchest supporters interacting directly with one of the very figures the president surely will denigrate onstage later.

“I’m going to ask that voter, those voters, what matters to them, because they actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said ahead of the president’s arrival for the evening event with Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Mississippi, among the nation’s most reliably Republican states, is not where the GOP envisioned needing a late-October stop from the president. But Hyde-Smith faces a stiff challenge from Colom, one of many Democratic underdogs that have managed to expand the House and Senate battleground maps because of widespread voter discontent over inflation, the Iran war and other aspects of Trump’s second presidency.

Colom said the dynamics make it easy for him to make a case to Trump rallygoers that Hyde-Smith is “not gonna change one single thing” that’s making voters’ lives harder.

“If you want somebody who’s gonna fight for higher wages, lower costs, get us out this stupid war, fight for affordable and accessible healthcare, actually stop the corruption that’s ruining our country, actually represent our Mississippi values, vote for Scott Colom,” he said.

Trump’s event with Hyde-Smith will kick off a week that continues to pit Trump against former President Barack Obama, the Democrat he first succeeded in 2017, and former Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democrat he defeated in 2024 to return to power. Trump’s itinerary has been taking him to many states that he won comfortably in 2024.

Democrats, including progressives, are expanding their efforts

Other top nominees and surrogates are greeting voters — almost 30 million of whom have already cast ballots — as Republicans scramble to protect their threadbare majority in the House, shore up a Senate majority that was once thought secure and maintain the GOP’s national advantage in state capitals.

Minnesota was the center of the progressive movement’s effort to leverage many Americans’ economic struggles, as Democratic Senate nominee Peggy Flanagan, the current lieutenant governor, welcomed House Progressive Caucus Chairwoman Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., to advocate for a national health insurance plan to achieve universal coverage.

“Everywhere I go on this tour I meet Minnesotans who are working hard and doing everything right and still can’t afford to take care of themselves or the people they love,” said Flanagan, who is backed by progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont. Flanagan is running against former sportscaster Michele Tafoya for the open seat.

If passed, the healthcare bill, which would include added benefits such as dental, vision, and hearing coverage, could save up to $1 trillion in healthcare spending, Jayapal said at the conference.

“We desperately need to build a completely different system and stop tinkering around the edges of a sick care system,” said Jayapal, who is the lead author and sponsor of the bill.

Harris was to campaign in neighboring Wisconsin with Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who faces Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Trump ally, for governor. Crowley would be the state’s first Black governor if elected to lead the battleground state.

In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms are getting an assist from Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, chairman of the Democratic Governors Association and a likely 2028 presidential candidate, two days after Trump made his second October visit to the state.

Vice President JD Vance was headed to Kansas on behalf of Sen. Roger Marshall, who finds himself locked in a tight contest with Democratic nominee and United Methodist megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932.

House Democrats also continue to expand their spending footprint, with the House Majority PAC announcing almost $2.5 million in new spending in Minnesota and Indiana districts that had been considered solid GOP territory earlier in the cycle.

The Minnesota seat has been reliably Republican for generations, other than a recent stretch when Tim Walz, the state’s two-term governor and Democrats’ 2024 vice presidential nominee, represented the sprawling, heavily rural district.

Trump to rally in another reliably Republican state

But it’s Trump’s visit to Mississippi that perhaps brings the midterm landscape into the sharpest relief with just a week of campaigning left before votes are tallied.

To be sure, Hyde-Smith, who is vying for her second full term, remains the favorite in a state Trump won three times by an average of nearly 20 percentage points.

But Colom, a local prosecutor who would make history as Mississippi’s first Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction, is looking to parlay inflation, Trump’s lagging popularity and Hyde-Smith’s mistakes into an upset.

Colom has outpaced Hyde-Smith in fundraising since he launched his campaign last year, and he caught national attention this month with an ad that played off Hyde-Smith dismissing beef prices — driven higher by Trump’s tariffs and fuel spikes resulting from the Iran conflict. The ad features Hyde-Smith, a former state agriculture commissioner, saying that consumers “have so many other proteins to choose from,” followed by several characters, and then Colom, saying Mississippi should “pick another senator instead.”

Colom’s campaign followed with a social media video that featured an AI-generated Hyde-Smith dodging questions about that controversy and other issues. The Democrat took down the video after the Mississippi attorney general said it could violate state law barring the use of deepfakes so close to Election Day.

Senate Democrats’ super PAC, meanwhile, has been a late entry in the contest, with a $1.2 million investment — a paltry sum compared with Senate contests in more populous states like Texas or Georgia but an amount that can go farther in Mississippi’s smaller television markets.

Mississippians have not chosen a new Democratic senator since 1947, and Democrats last won a Senate race there when that senator, the onetime segregationist John Stennis, won his last reelection in 1982.

South Carolina has emerged as another unexpectedly competitive Senate race where a Democratic victory by Dr. Annie Andrews over Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to succeed her late brother, would rank as a seismic upset.

Trump announced Monday that he’d be returning to the state on Thursday for his second general election visit on Graham’s behalf. Andrews, meanwhile, touted a bipartisan endorsement Monday from two former South Carolina governors, Republican David Beasley and Democrat Jim Hodges. Andrews’ campaign says more than 100 Republicans have joined her “Republicans for Annie” coalition.

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority, meaning Democrats must flip at least four seats for a change in control. The GOP began the cycle with a 220-215 advantage in the House, but a national gerrymandering fight made nine Democrats-held seats friendlier to Republicans based on 2024 presidential outcomes in those districts.

news.title: Minnesota Senate Race Shaken by ICE, Fraud and Ilhan Omar Probe
news.text: Republicans view the Minnesota Senate race as a potential pickup opportunity in the 2026 midterm elections, even as they face an increasingly difficult national environment in the final stretch of the campaign. The Minnesota Senate race shifted from Likely Democratic to Lean Democratic in the Cook Political Report as a flurry of recent polls showed a tight race between Democratic Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan and retired broadcaster Michele Tafoya, a Republican. While Republicans are dealing with challenging headwinds nationally, Democrats are having their own difficulties in Minnesota, experts told Newsweek. The race presents Republicans a pickup opportunity in a cycle that has been difficult for their party. Democrats have faced backlash over Democratic Governor Tim Walz’s handling of a fraud scandal in the general election, which has become a flash point in the Senate race, with Flanagan facing scrutiny over her proximity to Walz. Fraud and Corruption Among Top Issues There is "no doubt" the race is competitive as Flanagan has had a difficult time shaking the fraud backlash, Larry Jacobs, political scientist at the University of Minnesota, told Newsweek on Monday. "That's clearly tarnished her reputation, and her opponent comes back to it constantly," he said. David Schultz, professor of political science at Hamline University, told Newsweek that many voters view fraud and corruption, along with affordability, as among their top issues in Minnesota. "The question becomes if the voters are basically voting as a referendum on the incumbent party, is the incumbent in Minnesota Donald Trump or is it Governor Walz? Is it the fraud at the national level or at the state level? We don’t have enough data to parse that," he said. Minnesota is also the only competitive Senate race where a Republican candidate outraised the Democratic candidate in the third quarter of 2026, when Tafoya raised $4.3 million to Flanagan’s $3.8 million. The two are running to succeed Senator Tina Smith, a Democrat who is retiring at the end of her term. Newsweek reached out to the Flanagan and Tafoya campaigns for comment via email. Walz and Flanagan Under Fire The fraud scandal has become a sticking point for Democrats in Minnesota this year. Republican attacks have centered around a nonprofit called Feeding Our Future, which was implicated in a $250 million COVID-era scheme involving fraudulent claims for child nutrition programs. The Justice Department’s probe, which began under the Biden administration, has led to dozens of indictments, including members of Minnesota’s Somali community. Estimates of the cost to taxpayers have ranged from $250 million to $1 billion. Republicans accused Walz of inadequately responding to the scandal. They argued that his administration did not do enough to prevent the alleged fraud, but Walz’s office previously told Newsweek that he has "worked for years to crack down on fraud and asked the state Legislature for more authority to take aggressive action." Tafoya has tied Flanagan to the fraud scandal throughout the campaign. "Why has no one been fired? The only real consequence we've seen is that Tim Walz was convinced to step out of his third term gubernatorial race because there was no way he was going to survive this. But Peggy Flanagan's asking for a promotion," she said during an interview on The Wall Street Journal’s All Things with Kim Strassel podcast. Flanagan addressed fraud concerns in an interview with CBS News earlier in October. "I would say this: I am incredibly angry with the fraud as most Minnesotans are as well, but I have supported the independent Office of Inspector General and harsher penalties," she told the broadcaster. 'Fatigue' Over Democratic Rule in Minnesota Republicans believe they may benefit from "fatigue" with Democratic rule in the state, Schultz said. Democrats have been in control of the Minnesota governorship for 16 years. "What's going on here in the state is dueling narratives," he said. "Republicans are talking about Walz and fraud, and the Democrats are talking about Trump and fraud and corruption. The question becomes again, given her close association to Walz and his low approval ratings, how is it tainting her?" Kevin Parsneau, professor of political science at Minnesota State University, Mankato, told Newsweek that Tafoya doesn’t have "even odds" but does have a chance at flipping the seat. "There is some degree that the 2026 will be an anti-incumbent, anti-status quo election, in addition to being a referendum on Trump and Republican control at the federal level," he said. "In states that lean Democratic where they’ve held state government, that might help Republicans, especially one who hasn't been in politics." The fraud scandal, he said, has "given Republicans an issue to run on that resonates with Minnesota’s political culture that has a distaste for anything that smells of bad government." "It’s given Tafoya an issue to run on as an outsider with no political record other than general public support for Trump and some Republican policy positions. It gives Republicans a better chance than we would otherwise expect given the conventional wisdom that midterms are a referendum on the president," ’ he added. Operation Metro Surge Becomes GOP Vulnerability Meanwhile, Democrats have emphasized immigration as a major issue after the state became the epicenter of the Trump administration’s ramped-up immigration enforcement earlier this year. Two American citizens, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by federal immigration officers in January amid protests in Minneapolis, fueling anger over the White House's hard-line approach to immigration and border security. While there was more support for these operations in conservative, rural parts of the state, they were deeply unpopular in the Twin Cities, Schultz said. He said Operation Metro Surge likely "radicalized" Democrats to support Flanagan, a progressive, over moderate Representative Angie Craig in the primary. There may be signs of an energized voting base in early voting, he said. "It looks like Metro Surge may have motivated or energized the Democrats, which again works to the benefit of Flanagan in terms of her campaign," he said. Parsneau said that Republicans are vulnerable "to the extent that Democrats connect them to the Trump administration." "Like every other prominent Republican, Tafoya has a weakness on the issue because of supporting Trump and enabling what's seen as federal overreach," he said. Ilhan Omar Probe's Impact on Senate Race Minnesota politics was again upended earlier in October after the Washington-area home of Representative Ilhan Omar, a progressive Democrat representing Minneapolis, was raided amid an ongoing federal immigration probe. A warrant listed several potential immigration offenses under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, as well as a general conspiracy charge, The New York Times reported, citing a person familiar with the document. Newsweek has not independently reviewed the warrant. Omar has denounced the probe, describing it as an "attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement" in a post on X. Schultz said he believes the probe may "mobilize" Democrats. "If Trump's goal here was to try to damage Omar and therefore cause damage to Democrats, I think it's boomeranged," he said. Jacobs, meanwhile, cast doubt that there would be much of an impact either way. "It’s certainly an issue and I think it deserves attention. But no, I don't think it is playing into the Senate race," he said. Tafoya addressed the probe during an interview with Fox News, saying she is "running in a different race" and that there are people who are "concerned" about these allegations. "No one is above the law. This doesn’t impact my race as much, except for what you just said, that we had single party rule in Minnesota for so long, and we are going 100 miles per hour in the wrong direction. It has led to this fraud," she said. Is Minnesota a Blue State? Minnesota last voted for a Republican at the presidential level in 1972, but it has still been close in recent contests, giving Democrats only narrow victories. Former Vice President Kamala Harris carried the state by only about four points in 2024, a narrower win than former President Joe Biden’s seven-point victory in 2020. In 2016, Minnesota backed former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton by less than two percentage points. Former President Barack Obama did better in the state, carrying it by nearly eight points in 2012 and more than 10 points in 2008. Minnesota last elected a Republican senator in 2002, backing Norm Coleman. In 2008, he lost reelection to Democrat Al Franken. Flanagan's Progressive Views May Alienate Rural, Conservative Voters, Experts Warn Jacobs said Flanagan’s progressive policies could be a challenge in an evenly divided state, in addition to the fraud scandal. Despite its record of voting for Democrats in presidential races, it is still "pretty close to parity," he said. "There has been research that shows that candidates who are perceived as ideologically extreme in either party tend to get less support, you know, six to 10 points, maybe, depending on the race," he said. Flanagan has been endorsed by progressives like Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and has embraced left-wing policies like abolishing ICE and Medicare for All. She has also embraced calls to impeach Trump if Democrats win majorities in Congress. Minneapolis and St. Paul are both Democratic strongholds, and their suburbs have quickly shifted leftward over the past decade. But Republicans have still gained significant ground in the state’s vast, rural areas that used to be more competitive. Minnesota consistently votes to the left of other competitive Great Lakes states like Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Schultz said that Flanagan’s more progressive viewpoints make her "hugely unpopular" in Greater Minnesota. "She needs a big turnout in the Minneapolis-St. Paul metropolitan area and needs to hold her own in greater Minnesota," he said. "Luckily for her, probably about 56% of the vote is the greater metropolitan area of the Twin Cities, which leans very liberal." Minnesota Senate Race: What Polls, Odds Show Polling has shown a close race in Minnesota. Flanagan led by two points in RealClearPolitics’ polling aggregate as of Monday. An InsiderAdvantage poll last month showed Flanagan up a single point, 46 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 28 to 29, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.95 percentage points. Meanwhile, Flanagan led by four points in a Quantus Insights poll, 49 percent to 45 percent, among 720 likely voters from September 8 to 10. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. Prediction markets give Flanagan an edge. The Democratic candidate had an 84 percent chance of victory on Kalshi and an 86 percent chance on Polymarket as of Monday. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Sabato’s Crystal Ball, another key forecaster, also rates the race as Leans Democratic. They shifted the race from Likely Democratic on October 14. Analysts J. Miles Coleman and Kyle Kondik pointed to an "underwhelming" performance in polls. What Happens Next Early voting is underway in Minnesota as both parties consider the race to be competitive. The state will be closely watched over the coming days as Flanagan and Tafoya make their final pitches to undecided voters. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Robert Greenall and Jason Lemon
news.summary: Even as Republicans face tough national headwinds, they stand a chance at flipping Minnesota's Senate seat, experts told Newsweek.

news.title: Why is Texas so important? It’s about Senate control – and symbolism
news.text:
Lined up outside an event center in Fort Bend County, a few hundred supporters of Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton chat and smile in the cool October sun.

Some of those smiles are nervous.

“I’m worried,” admits Marlene Keplinger, as she waits to enter the rally in this well-manicured Houston suburb, where Mr. Paxton and his opponent, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, are vying for swing voters. Behind her, John Bickett says he’s worried, too.

“Talarico has lots of money. You see him on the TV every five minutes,” he adds.

Fort Bend used to be reliably Republican, but as it has grown and diversified, it has become more Democratic. In the 2024 presidential election, Kamala Harris narrowly defeated Donald Trump here.

When hundreds of Mr. Talarico’s supporters descend on the same venue just 24 hours after the Paxton event, the mood is noticeably more upbeat.

“This is a golden opportunity,” says Larry Junek, a retiree and longtime resident. He calls Mr. Talarico “compassionate” and someone who will help restore the role of Congress as a strong check on the presidency. Mr. Junek feels confident that Democrats are on the brink of winning their first statewide race in Texas in more than three decades.

“We have a president with ratings in the toilet, and we have the perfect candidate to run against in Ken Paxton,” he adds. A Talarico defeat, he continues, “would be hard to accept.”

It has become a biennial question in Texas: After three decades of Republican Party dominance, will this be the year Texas turns blue? The question keeps getting asked because, in recent elections, like Charlie Brown running toward Lucy holding the football, Texas Democrats have ended up flat on their backs.

Except maybe this year is the year. With the Paxton-Talarico contest, Democrats believe they have a unique opportunity to end their losing streak because of a confluence of factors – including Mr. Paxton’s history of political scandals; voter frustration with the economy under President Trump; and Mr. Talarico’s embrace of his Christian faith on the campaign trail. Republicans, meanwhile, are biting their nails over the prospect of suffering an embarrassing defeat in a state that has been the political and ideological heart of modern American conservatism.

An unusual year

For Mr. Paxton, it’s hard to imagine an electoral environment more unfavorable. He has close ties with the president and his endorsement, but Mr. Trump is facing record-low approval ratings. Voters are complaining about economic conditions, particularly high prices for necessities such as gas and groceries.

On top of that, Mr. Paxton is an unusually divisive candidate. His 10 years as state attorney general have been punctuated by scandal and allegations of criminality, including indictment for securities fraud and impeachment by the Republican-controlled state House over corruption allegations. (He was later acquitted by the Texas Senate.) His wife filed for divorce last year, alleging adultery.

His victory in the primary this year over more moderate incumbent Sen. John Cornyn symbolized a victory for the president’s MAGA base over the GOP establishment. Yet, to many political observers, the prediction that nominating a controversial candidate such as Mr. Paxton would put an otherwise safe seat in play has so far proved accurate.

“Had John Cornyn been nominated, we wouldn’t even be talking about Texas today,” says Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist and president of North Star Opinion Research.

Mr. Paxton’s supporters, however, contend that he’s a better fit for Texas. They point to Mr. Paxton’s long record of fighting for conservative causes, including issuing aggressive legal challenges against both the Obama and Biden administrations. The economy, they contend, was worse under former President Joe Biden, and they view Mr. Paxton’s scandals as private matters driven by political animus.

Reaching voters in the final days

Polls have consistently shown the race as a dead heat or with Mr. Talarico holding a narrow lead over Mr. Paxton. Both candidates are criss-crossing the state with fast-paced bus tours in the final week of campaigning.

In his closing statements to voters, Mr. Talarico has been emphasizing Mr. Paxton’s scandals, which he explicitly ties to voters’ economic concerns.

“We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis,” he says. “We are running against the embodiment of [that] crisis.”

Mr. Paxton is framing the election as nothing less than existential.

“We’re on a knife’s edge,” he said. “If we lose Texas, we lose America.”

The Paxton campaign has focused its closing attacks on some of Mr. Talarico’s controversial past comments, including videos of him saying “God is nonbinary” and that, according to science, there are six biological sexes. The candidate has since walked back such statements. But Republican critics say the comments show Mr. Talarico is more radical than his bipartisan, Christianity-themed rhetoric might suggest.

While the polls have given Democrats reason for optimism, the state’s political realities still make Mr. Paxton the slight favorite. Texas’s cities and suburbs have been getting bigger and bluer, but Republicans have been able to rely on strong performances in deep-red rural areas to win statewide elections. That reality is likely to prove true again this year, says Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican political consultant.

“We have the votes,” he says. “There are enough Republicans to eke out a victory, even in a tough year for Republicans.”

As goes Texas, so goes the GOP?

A defeat for Mr. Paxton would not only end the GOP’s decadeslong electoral winning streak here, but it could also determine which party controls the Senate for the final two years of Mr. Trump’s presidency. It would also represent a powerful symbolic defeat in a state that has become the touchstone of Republican America.

The clearest indication of the importance of the race is in campaign finance reports. The Paxton-Talarico contest is the most expensive in the country this cycle, with more than $500 million spent on the race as of this month. Elon Musk, whose SpaceX and Tesla companies are based in Texas, has donated $158 million toward efforts to keep the state in Republican hands. Mr. Talarico has outraised Mr. Paxton in small-dollar fundraising and benefited from funding by big Democratic donors such as LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman.

It might not just be control of the Senate that Republicans are fighting to preserve. Since the early 2000s, the American conservative movement has been closely linked with Texas Republicans. From George W. Bush’s compassionate conservatism to the rise of Sen. Ted Cruz and the tea party, to Mr. Paxton and the MAGA era, Texas Republicans like to boast of how American conservatives follow their lead. A prosperous state with light taxation and minimal regulations, Texas can be seen as a blueprint of the Republican vision for the entire country. A victory for Mr. Talarico would thus be a major symbolic defeat, analysts say.

It could also give Democrats a reason to invest in Texas in the 2028 presidential election, says Mr. Steinhauser, who previously worked for Senator Cornyn. That would further accelerate Texas becoming a truly competitive state electorally.

“If Texas goes blue in one or two races this cycle, it will open Pandora’s box for Democrats to go into Texas and not leave,” he says.

Waiting in line to see Mr. Paxton earlier this week, Ms. Keplinger recalls her party’s last close call in 2018, when Senator Cruz narrowly defeated former U.S. Rep. Beto O’Rourke. Though the GOP incumbent won, the enthusiasm and turnout that Mr. O’Rourke inspired in this area appeared to help Democrats win every countywide race in Fort Bend County.

“Conservatives got complacent,” she says. “Hopefully, that doesn’t happen again.”

While no Democrat won statewide in 2018, the party enjoyed one of its best elections in decades further down the ballot. It included a statehouse victory for a Central Texas political novice named James Talarico.
news.summary: The close Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton in Texas has unsettled conservatives used to three decades of statewide political dominance.
news.author: Henry Gass

news.title: Donald Trump Holds Mississippi Rally as GOP Anxiety Grows in Deep South
news.text: President Donald Trump is heading to a state where national Republicans rarely have to campaign on Monday night. Trump will rally in Corinth, Mississippi, for Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, who faces an unexpectedly competitive challenge from Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney from Columbus. Trump won the state by about 23 points in 2024 and will headline the event at the Crossroads Arena as Hyde-Smith fights to hold her seat. Democrats have grown increasingly optimistic about Colom, whose campaign has gained traction after an ad attacking Hyde-Smith on beef prices went viral. Although winning in a state Democrats have not carried since 1982 remains a challenge, Trump's approval rating in Mississippi has fallen to its lowest level of either term, giving Democrats another reason to see an opportunity. The party sent former Vice President Kamala Harris to Mississippi last Thursday to raise Colom's profile. If elected, he would become the state's first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction ended. Newsweek reached out to the Hyde-Smith and Colom campaigns for comment Monday. How to Watch Trump's Mississippi Rally The rally is at the Crossroads Arena, 2800 South Harper Road in Corinth. Doors open at 2:30 p.m. local time, the program begins at 4:30 p.m. and Trump is scheduled to speak at 6 p.m. Central, or 7 p.m. Eastern, according to the Republican Party's event page. Attendees have to register in advance, with a limit of four tickets per sign-up. Where the Mississippi Senate Race Stands A 365 Project poll taken October 21-22 by the Democratic firm Change Research had Hyde-Smith at 43 percent and Colom at 40 percent, with the margin of error at plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Independent Ty Pinkins, a lawyer, drew 6 percent, enough to matter in a race this tight. All of the public polling has come from Democratic-aligned firms, and averages still favor the incumbent. The Pollsmax average gave Hyde-Smith a lead of about 7 points and its model put her chances of winning at roughly 93 percent. Prediction market Kalshi had her near 89 percent on Monday. The Cook Political Report moved the race from Solid Republican to Likely Republican last week. Sabato's Crystal Ball and NBC News also have it at Likely Republican, while Inside Elections has it Solid Republican. Colom has been campaigning on healthcare cuts, beef and grocery prices and Hyde-Smith's support for Trump's tax and spending law. He responded to news of the rally by saying: "Hyde-Smith is scared and that's why she's sending Donald Trump down here," in a statement to Mississippi Today, and challenged Trump to a debate. Brandon Jones, a Mississippi Democratic strategist and former state representative who works on political campaigns for the SPLC Action Fund, said the incumbent has left an opening. "The public polling in this race has been close since last year and the Hyde-Smith campaign has been silent on the price of diesel, runaway inflation and the war in Iran," Jones told Newsweek, calling those issues the ones at the top of voters' minds. Gerard Henderson, Colom's campaign manager, told the Associated Press that the campaign has "the resources and momentum to win." Will Trump Help or Hurt Hyde-Smith? Trump's stop follows a Thursday visit from Harris, her second trip to Mississippi in the past year. Hyde-Smith welcomed the visit before it was even confirmed, telling reporters in Vicksburg last week that the president was trying to help and that she was fine with him coming. Hayes Dent, a Mississippi-based Republican strategist and president of Hayes Dent Public Strategies, told Newsweek that Trump's visit could cost Hyde-Smith votes but is unlikely to change the outcome of the race. "Given the drag on the ticket that Trump has now become, I believe he will probably hurt Cindy by 3 or 4 points, but it won't matter because she's an immensely popular senator here in the state," Dent said. "Trump is an outlier now, and he's about to become a lame duck." Jones read the visit as a sign of Republican worry. "President Trump is in Mississippi because Republicans believe Cindy Hyde-Smith is in trouble," he said. "This may be the first time a visit from Trump doesn't help the Republican candidate here. He'd probably still take Mississippi, but I'm not sure his voters are thrilled with him right now." Other Mississippi Republicans read the trip as a pure turnout play. Republican National Committee member Henry Barbour, a nephew of former Mississippi Governor Haley Barbour, told WLBT in Jackson that a big turnout favors Hyde-Smith, while a low one could put Colom in the Senate. Henry Barbur's brother, Austin Barbour, a longtime Republican operative in the state, made a similar point to The Hill, saying that "it's a turnout game as every election is." Hyde-Smith has a record of trailing Trump on the ballot. In 2020, she won her first full term by 10 points while he carried the state by more than 16, a 6-point gap. This year, Trump is not on the ballot and his approval rating in the state is underwater. She told reporters that the national Democratic visits show how red Mississippi is, and Republicans have folded Harris into their attack ads against Colom. Dent agreed, describing Harris and Senators Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia as "poison pills" for Democrats seeking support in a state like Mississippi. He said a Democrat hoping to compete statewide should be seen with law enforcement and focus on the Second Amendment and border security. Trump's Approval Rating in Mississippi Trump won Mississippi in 2024 by about 23 points over Harris, extending a Republican presidential streak in the state that dates to 1980. Civiqs' rolling tracker of registered voters now has his approval in Mississippi at 41 percent and his disapproval at 52 percent, a net rating of -11 as of October 21, the worst reading it has logged in the state across both of his terms. In March, the same tracker had Trump at 49 percent approval and 46 percent disapproval. His numbers bobbed around even through the spring, then went negative in June and have stayed there. Mississippi is still friendlier to Trump than the country as a whole. National polling averages compiled on October 22 had his approval near 36 percent and his disapproval above 61 percent, close to record lows for either of his terms. Pollsters and analysts have tied the decline in part to the war with Iran and tariff fights that have pushed up consumer prices. Corinth is in the state's 1st Congressional District, which Trump carried with 68 percent of the vote in 2024. Why Republicans Are Spending in Mississippi The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), the main super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, launched an ad campaign in the "low seven figures" in Mississippi last week, Semafor reported. By Sunday night the group had reserved $1.3 million in airtime, according to AdImpact data cited by NBC News, roughly matching the Senate Majority PAC's $1.2 million buy for Colom. The SLF ad casts Colom as too liberal, ties him to billionaire George Soros, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and hits him on transgender issues. Only two weeks earlier, SLF operatives had looked at Idaho, South Dakota and Mississippi and decided none of them needed money, Axios reported. One national Republican operative summed up the mood to the outlet in two sentences: "The wall has broken. The enemy is inside the fort." Mississippi's sum is small next to Ohio or Iowa. But it joins Kansas and South Carolina on a list of deep-red states where Republicans are now playing defense, and the race has seen nearly $8 million in ads from October 1 through Election Day on November 3, with Democrats outspending Republicans about $5 million to $2.7 million, according to CNN. Among the campaigns, Colom had outspent Hyde-Smith roughly $4.6 million to $3.2 million as of last week, according to AdImpact data cited by AP. Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith's campaign manager, told CNN that the senator had not asked her party for more resources. "We are confident that Senator Hyde-Smith will win on November 3rd," he said in a statement. Hyde-Smith waved off the late talk about polls as noise when reporters asked her last week. Senator Roger Wicker, the state's senior Republican senator, told Mississippi Today that Mississippi remains very much a Republican state at the federal level and that he believes Hyde-Smith still leads. "There's a lot of laws of physics in politics," Dent said. Once national Democrats and their outside groups move into a state, he argued, Republicans feel they have to match them, which he called "a natural sort of push, pull reaction to what the other side is doing." On the ground, he predicted, Hyde-Smith wins "by probably 10 points." For Jones, the spending itself is the story. "I think we all would have been surprised if someone had told us in January that President Trump was going to spend the waning days of the election trying to bail out a Republican incumbent in Mississippi," he said. "It's the latest indication that Democrats are probably about to win elections in places that no one saw coming." Black Voters Hold the Key for Colom Mississippi has the highest percentage of Black residents of any state, at nearly 38 percent. Colom would become the state's first Black U.S. senator since the end of Reconstruction, but getting there will require strong turnout among Black voters and support from white voters. A Democrat needs a large Black turnout and roughly one-quarter of the white vote to win, Mississippi NAACP Executive Director Charles Taylor told CNN. No Democrat has managed that combination in a Senate race since John C. Stennis in 1982. There are signs that Democrats could be making progress. Democratic primary turnout this year was up 90 percent from the previous cycle, and the NAACP's first major voter registration drive since 2012 added more than 17,000 people to the rolls, Taylor told CNN. Data for Progress found in an August survey that Black voters were more enthusiastic about voting than white voters, 43 percent to 31 percent. It estimated that Black voters made up just under 32 percent of the electorate. If their share rose to 35 percent, Hyde-Smith's 6-point lead in the model would shrink to 4. Jones set Colom's targets at about the same level. "To win, Colom will probably need Black voters to make up around 35 percent of the electorate and he'll need to win just over 25 percent of the white vote," he said. Terrance Woodbury, president of the Democratic research firm HIT Strategies, used the term "blacklash" in an interview with CNN to describe the backlash against Republican efforts to curb Black political power, including the push to dismantle Mississippi's 2nd Congressional District, represented in the U.S. House by Democrat Bennie Thompson. Dent is skeptical that Democrats can assemble a winning coalition. Few white Democrats remain in the state, he said, and "with African Americans having 37 percent of the statewide population, it's just simply not enough to carry the day." The coalition can work in legislative districts and Thompson's congressional district, Dent argued, "but not across the state." Turnout could be especially important because Mississippi has no early in-person voting. Only voters who qualify for absentee ballots can vote before Election Day, and in-person absentee voting closes at noon on Saturday. Trump and Vance Spend the Final Week in Red States After Corinth, Trump's closing schedule stays mostly in states he won comfortably in 2024: Lubbock and Corpus Christi, Texas, on Tuesday for Senate nominee Ken Paxton, then Chillicothe, Ohio, on Wednesday. He heads to Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday and to Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday, alongside Senate candidate Ashley Hinson. Vice President JD Vance holds rallies on Monday in Belgrade, Montana, and also in Topeka, Kansas, where Senator Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, a week after Trump rallied near Wichita. Vance goes to Weatherford, Texas, on Thursday. His one swing-state stop this week is Howell, Michigan, on Tuesday. Trump has pitched these trips as turnout drives, telling crowds at earlier rallies to vote as if he were on the ballot. news.summary: A competitive Mississippi U.S. Senate race no one expected is drawing Trump, Kamala Harris and GOP money. Can the Democrat win?
