news.title: Republicans on Defense in Districts GOP Redrew to Win Midterm: Full List
news.text: Republicans redrew dozens of congressional districts to become more friendly to conservatives ahead of the midterms in hopes of averting losses. But many of those seats are emerging as competitive battlegrounds as the national environment becomes increasingly challenging for the GOP in the final stretch of the campaign. House districts in Alabama, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas became much more conservative in mid-decade redistricting. Many of these previously competitive or Democratic-leaning seats now backed President Donald Trump by double digits under their new lines. But Republican hopes that these seats would be easy pickups have dimmed. The Cook Political Report’s latest ratings consider many of these seats to be competitive despite their new conservative lean, as Democrats hope to expand the battleground to compete in tougher seats. These races have become competitive as Trump’s approval rating has fallen to record lows in the past few weeks. Democrats have also seen a strong lead in the generic ballot, a gauge of the House popular vote, leading by 8.3 points in RealClearPolitics’ polling aggregate as of Monday. The Cook Political Report has shifted numerous races toward Democrats in the past few weeks and has signaled that they view Democrats as favorites to retake the House. Many of the latest changes come from districts that backed Trump by double digits in 2024. Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) spokesperson Bridget Gonzalez wrote in a statement to Newsweek, "House Republicans thought they could ruin the economy, raise the cost of everything, and then rig the maps to save their seats. They’re going to get crushed in November and they have only themselves to blame." Newsweek also reached out to the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) for comment via email. Republicans on Defense in These Redrawn Districts Recent forecasts show that these seats, many of which are drawing significant investment from both major parties, are part of the midterm battleground. These races are competitive, meaning Republicans could still win, but they have not been easy pickups due to a more favorable environment for Democrats. But even if Democrats do not win, these seats have drawn investments from Republicans that could have otherwise gone to other races in more traditionally competitive seats. In addition to drawing out Democrats, Republicans also hoped to shore up their own incumbents by putting them in more conservative seats. Most of those changes were modest, and these incumbents are now facing challenging reelection bids. On the other hand, there are some Democratic-held districts based around Dallas, Texas; Memphis, Tennessee; and Louisiana that became more conservative in redistricting and are not seen as competitive, so Republicans are favored to pick up at least a few seats from the effort. Alabama Following the Supreme Court ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, which found Louisiana violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause by drawing a second majority-Black congressional district, lawmakers in Alabama redrew the state’s map to place Democratic Representative Shomari Figures in a more conservative district. His district went from spanning the Black Belt and leaning Democratic to being a double-digit Trump seat based around Montgomery and more conservative southeastern Alabama. But the race is still seen as competitive, with the Cook Political Report classifying the race as Lean Republican. Florida Florida’s congressional map changed significantly during redistricting. Several Democrats were placed in more Republican-leaning seats, and purple districts represented by Republicans became more conservative. The changes followed a political transformation in the Sunshine State, which shifted from a true battleground to a Republican stronghold over the past decade amid an influx of conservative retirees and a rightward shift among Hispanic voters. Florida’s 13th District, based around Pinellas County, became slightly more conservative in redistricting as GOP Representative Anna Paulina Luna faces a challenge from Democrat Leela Gray. Trump won the seat by 13 points, a slight rightward shift from Trump’s 11 point victory on the current map. It’s seen as Lean Republican by the Cook Political Report. Representative Kathy Castor, a Democrat, is among the lawmakers who saw the most significant changes to her district based around Tampa, which lost areas more friendly to Democrats for more conservative suburbs and rural areas. Trump won the seat by 10 points, but it is a toss-up. Florida’s 22nd, based around South Florida, is another that changed significantly, losing more liberal areas in southeastern Florida. It now spans across the southern part of the state to take in conservative areas near Naples, backing Trump by 10 points. The race between Democrat Pia Dandiya and Republican Casey Askar is a toss-up. Florida’s 25th District was purple under the previous map, only narrowly backing former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. Under the new lines, it went to Trump by nine points. Cook gives Democratic Representative Jared Moskowitz an edge over Republican Scott Singer, classifying it as Lean Democratic. North Carolina North Carolina Republicans sought to put Democratic Representative Don Davis in a tougher seat that backed Trump by nearly 12 points, compared to roughly three points on the current map. But it’s still considered close, with the Cook Political Report classifying it as a toss-up. Lawmakers swapped counties between North Carolina’s 1st District, historically a more Democratic district with a high Black population represented by Davis, with North Carolina’s 3rd District, held by GOP Representative Greg Murphy. That district shifted from giving Trump a 22-point victory in 2024 to a 14-point victory under the new map. It’s rated Likely Republican by Cook. Ohio Two Democratic-held seats in Ohio became more conservative. Ohio’s 1st District, held by Democratic Representative Greg Landsman, lost areas around Cincinnati for its conservative suburbs. It went from giving Harris a six-point victory in 2024 to backing Trump by about three points. It’s considered to be Likely Democratic by the Cook Political Report. Meanwhile, in Ohio’s 9th District, based around Toledo and northwestern Ohio, Democratic Representative Marcy Kaptur is facing a toss-up race against Republican Derek Merrin. That district went from backing Trump by seven points to more than 10 points in redistricting. Two Republicans in purple seats were also given slightly more conservative lines but are facing competitive races. In Ohio’s 10th District, Republican Representative Mike Turner is in a Lean Republican race against Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker. The district went from Trump +6 to Trump +8 in redistricting, according to Inside Elections. Meanwhile, GOP Representative Mike Carey’s district went from about Trump +9 to Trump +10, according to Inside Elections. It’s considered to be Lean Republican. Texas In Texas, the first state to redraw its maps ahead of the midterms, Republican gains could be chilled by a potential reversion back to Democrats among Hispanic voters. Several South Texas districts were redrawn to become more conservative. That includes two that are held by Democrats, TX-28, held by Representative Henry Cuellar and TX-34, held by Representative Vicente Gonzalez. Cook favors Democrats in both seats, rating TX-28 as Likely Democratic and TX-34 as Lean Democratic. Meanwhile, TX-35, which has been based around Austin and San Antonio, shifted from a solidly Democratic stronghold to having a more conservative lean, backing Trump by about 10 points under the current map. It’s rated as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report. Democrats’ Chances of Flipping House: What Polls Show Polling has given Democrats an advantage on the generic ballot. Historically, when the president is unpopular, his party loses seats in the midterms. Such was the case during Trump’s first term in 2018, when Democrats flipped more than 40 House seats. Democrats have worked to make the race a referendum on Trump’s presidency as his approval slips due to economic anxiety among the electorate centered around high prices and affordability. The latest poll from YouGov and CBS News gave Democrats an eight-point lead on the generic ballot, 53 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 2,355 likely voters from October 21 to 23, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points. The latest polling data from The New York Times and Siena University, conducted among 3,494 likely voters from October 12 to 19, showed Democrats up 11 points, 52 percent to 41 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 1.9 percentage points. Former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, a California Republican, told Bloomberg News last week he believes Democrats are likely to retake the House. "In the last 100 years, all off-year elections, whoever is the party in power, has the White House, has lost seats, and it’s only a few seats for the majority," he said. "It won’t be like when Obama was in when we won 63 seats, or when Clinton was in and for the first time in 40 years, Republicans took over. They’ll get a majority. I’m not quite sure how big it is. But they will probably win the majority." How Have Recent House Elections Gone? Recent House elections have been close, with 2018 being the most recent "blue wave" year, when Democrats picked up dozens of seats during the midterm of Trump’s first term in office. Democrats believe this year could yield similar results if these critical toss-up races break their way. Here is a look at how recent elections have gone. What Happens Next With only about one week until November 3, candidates are likely to spend the final days of the campaign making their cases to voters in hopes of winning over undecided voters and motivating their base to head to the polls. Early voting is already underway in many states. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. news.title: Trumpu ključna kontrola Senata, demokratima adut standard
news.text:
Rekordno niska popularnost američkog predsjednika Donalda Trumpa još otkako mu je počeo drugi mandat, nezadovoljstvo birača zbog rasta troškova života i sporovi oko imigracije obilježavaju međuizbore 2026. u SAD-u, na kojima će birači 3. studenoga odlučiti hoće li republikanci zadržati kontrolu nad Kongresom ili će demokrati dobiti veće mogućnosti za osporavanje i blokiranje poteza Trumpove administracije.

Cijena goriva, cijena izbora

Republikanci uoči međuizbora imaju tijesnu većinu u oba doma američkog Kongresa – u Zastupničkom domu vode s 218 prema 214 mjesta, a u Senatu imaju većinu od 53 prema 47. Demokratima je potreban neto dobitak od četiri mjesta kako bi preuzeli kontrolu nad svakim od tih domova. Ishod će ovisiti o malom broju neizvjesnih izbornih utrka, a na kampanju na nacionalnoj razini znatno će utjecati i sam Trump. 

U završnici predizborne kampanje Trump nastoji privući pozornost birača i mobilizirati svoje pristaše. Prema anketi Reutersa i Ipsosa, stopa odobravanja njegova rada pala je na povijesno niskih 31 posto. Unatoč tome, više je puta pozvao birače da se ponašaju kao da se i sam natječe na izborima. Takva bi poruka mogla potaknuti demokrate i neovisne birače da se ujedine protiv republikanaca, no Trump nastoji povećati izlaznost vlastitih pristaša.

Demokrati ističu da Trump nije ispunio obećanja o snižavanju troškova života i okončanju ratova. Najavljuju mjere za smanjenje životnih troškova i veću dostupnost osnovnih dobara i usluga te poručuju da će, preuzmu li kontrolu nad jednim od domova Kongresa, pozvati Trumpovu administraciju na odgovornost zbog korupcije.

Rast troškova života i dalje je jedna od glavnih bolnih točaka za američke birače. Polovina registriranih, obuhvaćenih nedavnom anketom Reutersa i Ipsosa, navela je troškove života kao presudan čimbenik pri odabiru kandidata. Među troškovima na koje bi se zakonodavci trebali usredotočiti izdvojili su zdravstvenu skrb, gorivo, hranu i stanovanje.

Cijene goriva naglo su porasle nakon što su Sjedinjene Američke Države i Izrael u veljači pokrenuli vojne napade na Iran. Prema podacima Američkog automobilskog udruženja (AAA), prosječna cijena benzina na nacionalnoj razini iznosi 4,28 dolara po galonu, što je 1,20 dolara više nego prije godinu dana. Dizel u prosjeku stoji 6,32 dolara po galonu, odnosno 2,7 dolara više nego godinu prije.

Podaci Ureda za statistiku rada upućuju na rast cijena namirnica od 1,8 posto u posljednjih godinu dana, dok su, prema podacima Savezne agencije za stambeno financiranje, cijene nekretnina u istom razdoblju porasle za 2,1 posto. Kongres je početkom ove godine usvojio međustranački zakon o stanovanju, koji je stupio na snagu bez Trumpova potpisa.

Kao glavni dosadašnji zakonodavni uspjeh republikanci ističu produljenje poreznih olakšica. U sklopu istog zakonskog paketa predviđeno je smanjenje javne potrošnje za približno bilijun dolara, ponajprije za Medicaid, program zdravstvenog osiguranja namijenjen građanima s niskim primanjima, i druge zdravstvene programe. Demokrati su se prošle godine pokušali izboriti za produljenje subvencija za zdravstveno osiguranje, kojima se koristilo 24 milijuna Amerikanaca, ali im je u međuvremenu istekao rok. Zbog toga su izazvali blokadu rada savezne vlade, no nisu uspjeli ostvariti svoj cilj.

Imigracijska politika također bi mogla imati važnu ulogu u predizbornoj borbi, osobito zbog spornih postupaka saveznih službenika i podjela oko njihova financiranja. Na području imigracije Trumpova administracija hvali se rezultatima strože granične politike. Prema preliminarnim podacima Ministarstva domovinske sigurnosti, broj migranata privedenih na jugozapadnoj granici smanjio se za 95 posto u odnosu na razdoblje administracije bivšeg predsjednika Joea Bidena. Ministarstvo je objavilo i da granična policija tijekom cijele fiskalne godine prvi put u povijesti nije pustila nijednog migranta na slobodu.

Međutim, u Maineu, Minnesoti i Teksasu zabilježeni su smrtonosni incidenti u kojima su sudjelovali savezni imigracijski službenici. Smrt dvoje američkih državljana u Minnesoti izazvala je snažne reakcije i potaknula mnoge demokratske kandidate u neizvjesnim stranačkim predizborima da zauzmu ljevije političke stavove. Neki su zatražili opoziv tadašnje ministrice domovinske sigurnosti Kristi Noem, dok su drugi pozvali na ukidanje Službe za imigraciju i carine (ICE). Koplja su se ove godine lomila i oko financiranja imigracijskih službi. 

Zbog zastoja u pregovorima republikanci su samostalno usvojili zakon vrijedan 70 milijardi dolara za financiranje ICE-a i granične policije do kraja Trumpova predsjedničkog mandata. Na kritike demokrata odgovaraju tvrdnjom da podupiru otvorene granice. Savezni imigracijski službenici ovoga su mjeseca pretresli dom demokratske zastupnice Ilhan Omar iz Minnesote u Washingtonu, što je izazvalo osudu demokrata. Prema riječima osobe upoznate sa slučajem, istraga bi mogla imati dalekosežnije posljedice za Omar, a jedan od mogućih ciljeva navodno je oduzimanje njezina američkog državljanstva i deportacija. 

Ulaganja u razvoj umjetne inteligencije i izgradnju podatkovnih centara, utjecaj kriptoindustrije, pravo na pobačaj i odnos prema Izraelu također bi mogli utjecati na birače u pojedinim izbornim utrkama. U utrci za Senat u Ohiju demokratski kandidat Sherrod Brown optužio je republikanskog senatora Jona Husteda da pogoduje tvrtkama koje ulažu u podatkovne centre. Istodobno je politički odbor povezan s kriptoindustrijom Defend American Jobs potrošio više od 46 milijuna dolara kako bi pomogao Hustedov reizbor i smanjio Brownove izglede za pobjedu. Brown je bivši senator koji je nekoć vodio senatski Odbor za bankarstvo.

Pobačaj, kripto i Izrael

U Maineu se demokratski kandidat Troy Jackson nada da birači neće zaboraviti da je republikanska senatorica Susan Collins podržala imenovanje Bretta Kavanaugha, konzervativnog suca Vrhovnog suda koji je 2022. podržao ukidanje ustavnog prava na pobačaj na saveznoj razini. Tom je odlukom pitanje reguliranja pobačaja prepušteno saveznim državama.

U Michiganu se demokratski kandidat Abdul El-Sayed na izborima za Senat natječe protiv republikanca Mikea Rogersa. El-Sayed je na stranačkim predizborima pobijedio demokratsku zastupnicu Haley Stevens, koju je financijski podupirao proizraelski politički odbor. El-Sayed je kritizirao izraelsku vojnu operaciju u Gazi, nazvao je genocidom i zauzimao se za prekid američke vojne pomoći Izraelu. Nakon njegova pobjedničkog ishoda na predizborima, odbor je potrošio više od 280 tisuća dolara na letke protiv njega.

Podsjetimo, Trump je nedavno podržao izraelskog premijera Benjamina Netanyahua u nastojanju da osvoji novi mandat na čelu izraelske vlade. Iako Zastupnički dom i Senat imaju jednaku zakonodavnu snagu, kontrola Senata u praksi je važnija zbog njegove uloge u potvrđivanju predsjedničkih imenovanja i ratificiranju međunarodnih ugovora. Demokrati imaju veće izglede preuzeti kontrolu nad Zastupničkim domom, dok je ishod utrke za Senat znatno neizvjesniji, ocijenio je politički analitičar i izvanredni profesor Višeslav Raos s Fakulteta političkih znanosti Sveučilišta u Zagrebu.

“Imenovanja koja predlaže predsjednik mogu se blokirati u Senatu, a za njihovu potvrdu potrebna je odgovarajuća većina. I međunarodni ugovori, bilo gospodarske, bilo sigurnosne naravi, također zahtijevaju odobrenje Senata”, istaknuo je Raos.

Prema njegovim riječima, projekcije upućuju na veliku vjerojatnost da će demokrati osvojiti većinu u Zastupničkom domu, dok je situacija u Senatu znatno neizvjesnija. To je važno i za predsjednika Donalda Trumpa, koji bi u slučaju gubitka republikanske kontrole nad jednim ili oba doma Kongresa imao znatno manje prostora za provedbu svojeg programa. Raos je podsjetio i na Trumpov prvi predsjednički mandat, kada su republikanci kontrolirali oba doma Kongresa, ali ni tada predsjedniku nije uspijevalo progurati sve najavljene zakonske promjene.

“Glavna stvar koju je Trump tada želio napraviti bilo je ukidanje Obamacarea, odnosno paketa zakona kojim je reformirano zdravstveno osiguranje. Međutim, to nije uspio progurati čak ni u situaciji u kojoj su republikanci imali većinu u oba doma jer se dio republikanaca nije slagao s njegovim zamislima”, rekao je Raos.

Ekonomija presudna biračima

Ostvare li demokrati uspjeh na predstojećim međuizborima, Trumpu će biti još teže provoditi političke planove kroz Kongres, dodao je Raos, koji smatra da bi predsjednik u takvim okolnostima mogao češće posezati za izvršnim uredbama, što bi otvorilo prostor za nove pravne sporove oko granica predsjedničkih ovlasti i pitanja što predsjednik smije poduzimati bez odobrenja Kongresa, osobito kada je riječ o vojnim intervencijama. Ističe da su u SAD-u gospodarske prilike snažnije povezane s raspoloženjem birača nego u Hrvatskoj i drugim državama Europske unije. Prema istraživanju centra Pew Research, na koje se pozvao, 84 posto birača smatra da je gospodarsko stanje važno pri odlučivanju o tome za koga će glasovati.

“Trump je nastojao sniziti inflaciju, no birači i dalje osjećaju pritisak troškova života”, kazao je. Prema Raosovoj procjeni, američki su birači posebno osjetljivi na rast cijena, uključujući cijene goriva i drugih energenata. “U Hrvatskoj i drugim državama Europske unije spremniji smo prihvatiti više stope inflacije i rast cijena goriva, dok su američki birači osjetljiviji na takva kretanja”, ocijenio je.

Na raspoloženje birača utječu i cijene energenata. Raos je u tom kontekstu spomenuo Trumpove poteze povezane s Rusijom i mogućim promjenama u opskrbi energentima. Takvi bi potezi mogli biti povezani s nastojanjem da se prije izbora stabiliziraju cijene nafte i plina, no pitanje je koliko će u tome biti uspješni i kakvi se interesi pritom isprepleću. Pritom je upozorio na moguće sukobe interesa povezane s poslovnim apetitima pojedinih ulagača bliskih Trumpovoj administraciji i njegovoj obitelji, ističući da motive takvih poteza treba promatrati i u tom kontekstu. 

Ocijenio je da demokrati u kampanji najveći naglasak stavljaju na troškove stanovanja i energenata te sve teže podmirivanje životnih troškova. Republikanci, pak, nastoje pridobiti birače isticanjem sigurnosti i energetske politike, uvjeravajući ih da Trumpova administracija može ponuditi rješenja za probleme koji ih najviše pogađaju. Na odluke američkih birača mogla bi utjecati i zbivanja u Europi, smatra Raos. Američka javnost prati događaje na europskom kontinentu, uključujući prosvjede i incidente obilježene nasiljem u Francuskoj. Takvi prizori mogli bi kod dijela birača pojačati osjećaj nesigurnosti i potaknuti ih da se priklone postojećoj vlasti, odnosno da glasuju za očuvanje statusa quo.

Prijevremeno glasovanje traje već tjednima, a bude li izlaznost slična onoj na međuizborima 2022., na birališta bi ove godine moglo izaći više od 100 milijuna Amerikanaca. To je ipak manje od 155 milijuna birača, koliko ih je glasovalo na predsjedničkim izborima 2024. godine.

Prema podacima tvrtke AdImpact, do 12. listopada na političke oglase emitirane u sklopu kampanja potrošeno je rekordnih 3,8 milijardi dolara. Najviše se ulagalo u neizvjesne utrke za Senat u Teksasu, Ohiju i Michiganu. Među najvećim financijerima republikanskih kandidata bio je Elon Musk, koji je za njihovu potporu potrošio oko 366 milijuna dolara.

Izborna povijest pokazuje da međuizbori mogu znatno promijeniti odnos snaga u Kongresu. Na izborima 2010., tijekom mandata demokratskog predsjednika Baracka Obame, republikanci su osvojili 63 dodatna mjesta u Zastupničkom domu i preuzeli kontrolu nad tim domom.

Njihovu uspjehu pridonijeli su slabi gospodarski rezultati i nezadovoljstvo Obaminom reformom zdravstvenog sustava. Demokrati su, međutim, zadržali većinu u Senatu, iako su izgubili šest mjesta. Obama je rezultat opisao kao težak poraz, nakon čega se suočio s republikanskim zahtjevima za znatnim smanjenjem državne potrošnje izvan obrambenog sektora. news.text:
CBS veteran Dan Rather has called his former network a "disaster" and charged that its leadership has turned it into a version of Fox News.

Rather, who turns 95 on Saturday, didn’t hold back over the changes at CBS News in an interview with Variety published Monday. He argued that President Trump and corporate interests have been the beneficiaries of the shake-up.

He described it as "in many ways a disaster," with the damage going well beyond the employees who were still working at the network.

He blamed the turmoil on the increasing influence of billionaires in American journalism and their ties to political power.

He was very specific in his criticism of CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, accusing her of taking the network down the path of becoming "a version of Fox News" since she'd taken over the newsroom.

“You judge a person by what they do, and what she’s done is she’s quickly turned CBS News in the direction of being a version of Fox News, perhaps a little more palatable," he said. "But I didn’t know her beforehand, and I don’t know her now. Frankly, we didn’t hear much about her until she was rewarded with many millions of dollars for her company and then paid to come in and start destroying CBS News.”

Weiss was appointed following the 2025 completion of the Skydance merger with Paramount, the parent company of CBS, by billionaire David Ellison. Ellison is a Trump ally, and Weiss had previously founded The Free Press, which Paramount acquired.

Rather maintained that the new ownership had enabled Trump to do something he'd long desired, namely to damage 60 Minutes, the investigative program that the president has lashed out against repeatedly. 

"The wreckage of CBS News is everywhere," Rather declared, warning that the changes were still continuing and that they would be very difficult to reverse.

His comments come after months of turmoil at 60 Minutes, with long-serving correspondents Scott Pelley and Sharyn Alfonsi among those axed as part of a massive management shake-up.

Both were praised by Rather for standing up to the changes they felt would undermine the program's journalistic independence, especially Pelley, who took the opportunity to publicly challenge the new management.

He said journalists needed to "start challenging the power," even if that meant there were professional consequences for speaking out.

Pelley had previously accused management of introducing political bias into CBS reporting. CBS News has denied the allegations of political interference, stating that editorial decisions were made with the intent of improving both accuracy and fairness.

The standoff also comes on the back of Paramount's controversial $16 million settlement of Trump's lawsuit over the 2024 60 Minutes interview with former Vice President Kamala Harris. Paramount didn't issue an apology as part of that settlement.

Rather previously criticized the settlement as a surrender to the president's pressure, and he now goes on to criticize the direction of the network.

The former CBS Evening News anchor, who spent 24 years at the network, made it perfectly clear that his criticism was aimed at management, not at the many journalists who are still with the network.

news.title: Obama Polls That Will Drive Trump Wild
news.text:
Barack Obama continues to eclipse Donald Trump’s popularity, underlining the gulf between the two presidents as they trade blows on the final stretch of the midterm campaign.

With eight days until Election Day, a slew of polls continue to put the Democrat stalwart ahead of Trump among Americans, including all-important independent voters.

“Let’s just say that President Obama absolutely crushes President Trump when it comes to who is more liked by the American public,” CNN’s data guru Harry Enton said as he outlined one of the polls on Monday: aYouGov/Yahoo poll that put Obama’s approval at 55 percent compared to Trump at 37 percent.

The grim assessment comes days after Obama held his first two rallies of the 2026 midterm cycle, prompting Trump to issue a midnight tirade attacking his longstanding nemesis.

In Ohio, where the Daily Beast spent the weekend on the campaign trail, enthusiastic crowds queued up for hours, with lines stretching around several downtown blocks, to get into the Cleveland Public Auditorium, which has a capacity of 10,000.

In Detroit, more than 4,300 supporters packed a school gymnasium as Obama raged against the administration’s lawlessness, corruption, and economic failures. He also accused Republicans of trying to smear Democrats as “radicals, communists, jihadists, woke police.”

“We have seen this movie before, I starred in it,” Obama said, pushing back against attacks on El-Sayed that echoed the smears once directed at Obama himself.

A CNN/SSN survey conducted in June had Obama holding a 57 percent favorable rating among Americans surveyed, compared with 34 percent for Trump. 

In an open-ended question asking which president they admired most, 30 percent named Obama, compared with 19 percent who named Trump—an 11-point gap. 

Another UMASS/YouGov poll from earlier this year had Obama leading Trump by 23 percentage points in favorability. 

Among independents, only 31 percent viewed Trump favorably, while 68 percent viewed him unfavorably. 

“I wouldn’t be surprised if this margin has actually grown a little, as President Trump has been even less popular than he was at the start of this year,” Enten said.

The figures may partly explain Trump’s ongoing rage against Obama, such as the midnight Truth Social post he issued over the weekend.

The lengthy Truth Social post slammed Obama as a “grossly incompetent President”; resurrected Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris’s election defeats, and branded Michigan’s Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed a “Fake Doctor” and “Jihadist” who hates “Jews and Blacks and AMERICANS and TRUMP.”

“He said that Crooked Hillary Clinton was going to WIN, he campaigned hard for her, and she lost in all directions and ways. He then campaigned full out for Kamala, and likewise, she lost,” Trump wrote in a 12:42 a.m. post.

The post came not long after Obama had also unleashed a blistering attack on the administration, accusing the president of enriching himself and mocking the 80-year-old’s vanity projects.

“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a cheesecake factory!” he said to roars of laughter.

Obama delivered the remarks Saturday at a rally in support of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, a former top health director who was the target of a vicious MAGA attack ad, and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is trying to unseat Ohio’s GOP incumbent, former college football player, and object of Trump’s affection, Jon Husted.

news.text:
As Democrats warned, Project 2025 would undo decades of progress. The 920-page proposal became the blueprint for transforming the federal government and has become reality under President Donald Trump’s second administration. But the agenda appears to be backfiring, as former supporters across the country increasingly turn against Trump. Kamala Harris warned during her 2024 campaign that the agenda was designed to "weaken the middle class,” and as unemployment rates skyrocket, inflation continues. As DEI efforts are washed away, many agree with Harris’ sentiments. 

Although Trump initially tried to distance himself from Project 2025 amid public opposition to the plan, he ultimately brought its key architects into his administration to help carry it out. In the first 21 months of his second term, a USA Today report examines how much of the controversial blueprint has been implemented.

Project 2025 proposed that FEMA, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, hand off responsibility for disaster response to the states. Trump countered that by using FEMA funding as political leverage in blue states. FEMA’s Administrator Cameron Hamilton recently gave state officials the order that it’s not up to them to begin building up their emergency funds and resources to handle most disasters.

"One of the most surprising features of this administration has been the outright, unabashed politicization of emergency aid," notes William Galston, a senior fellow at The Brookings Institution, a nonpartisan research think tank. "That used to be one of the few remaining areas of genuine neutrality."

However, there is still some hope: many of Trump’s Project 2025 policies were enacted through executive orders, which a future president could reverse or rescind. The damage can still take time to recover from, but these policies and their effects have not fared well with the American public.

Another major area of concern has been significant job loss. Under Project 2025’s then-Elon Musk-run Department of Government Efficiency (DODGE), hundreds of thousands of positions were cut from the federal workforce, many of them with voluntary incentives for employees to quit, such as large payouts. Many of those positions are in the process of being restored, so the immediate effect cannot be measured.

As the report notes, DOGE is now widely viewed as a “sad joke.” Initially, the initiative claimed to have saved $215 billion in federal spending through job cuts and other measures. However, the Government Accountability Office reported this summer that those savings claims were largely unsubstantiated.

Trump’s biggest target was seemingly anything related to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI), which Elaine Kamarck, another Brookings Institute senior fellow, says has been largely effective. But Galston says businesses across the country have found a loophole: changing the way they identify the roles to keep their staff, thus questioning whether Trump’s implemented practices have long-standing power. Overall, the idea is that conservatives want control, but in their quest, what they’ve done may be counterproductive in the long term.

news.title: Joe Biden’s Worst Decision Is Even More Stunning When You Know How He Made It
news.text:
Nearly two years after leaving office, the officials who helped shape Joe Biden’s Gaza policy are beginning to tell their versions of what happened, often emphasizing what they tried to prevent rather than what they allowed to happen. Kamala Harris has 107 Days, Brett McGurk has Brink, and former White House press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre has Independent.But the consequences of their decisions, including the destruction of Gaza and the political fractures they left within the Democratic Party, have proved harder to escape. Public opinion has undergone a remarkable shift as Democratic voters now sympathize with Palestinians over Israelis by a ratio of nearly 4 to 1, and the issue has become consequential in many key 2026 races.

Akbar Shahid Ahmed, a longtime foreign-policy journalist, has spent more than two years assembling a record of those decisions. His new book, Crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel’s War in Gaza, draws on more than 150 interviews with government officials and extensive additional reporting. The result is a painstaking reconstruction of how Biden and a small circle of advisers repeatedly declined to use American leverage to restrain Israel, even as other officials warned of the consequences. I called Ahmed to ask what his reporting reveals about Biden’s personal responsibility and what Democrats can learn for the future. This interview has been edited and condensed clarity.

Aymann Ismail: Your reporting suggests that Biden’s own advisers controlled much of what reached him and what didn’t, and that colored the inaction we saw during the early days of Gaza. 

Akbar Shahid Ahmed: I really document how the normal functions of government, everyone weighing in, ambassadors abroad weighing in to create a foreign policy, was not happening on Israel. What this means is that Biden was listening to a really small group of people, his foreign policy advisers, but also his political brain trust. These are people who have two defining characteristics: a real, bone-deep loyalty to Biden personally, and a quite dated view of the electorate and this fixation on the idea of questioning Israel as politically toxic.

Biden is almost like a shadow or a ghost figure in this book. He looms over everything but is not actively pushing things in so many ways. They were making their own calculations way down the chain, very often without the president’s knowledge of what would get up to him and how. People who were involved in doing the president’s daily briefs—the intelligence, of course, went to Biden daily—felt that there was self-censorship and stifling. That’s not coming at the directive of the president. That’s coming from the environment in the administration.

One of the officials in that small circle was Brett McGurk, who’s much less familiar to the public than Antony Blinken, Biden’s secretary of state, or Jake Sullivan, his national security adviser. McGurk just published a new book about his experience in the administration. What do you think of his account?

Brett McGurk is extremely important to this story. He was the Middle East coordinator for Biden, with unprecedented power. Biden also had an Asia coordinator. He also had senior officials working on Europe. None of them were granted the kind of license to run their portfolio in the way that Biden and Jake Sullivan allowed Brett McGurk to dominate U.S. policy. I think sometimes people look at these policies and think some of these top officials are just deeply committed to Israel. McGurk had a broader commitment to American militarism and a commitment to, these are our partners, these are our guys, how dare you question them over human rights?

My reporting shows this was his approach in the administration post–Oct. 7, in so many of the discussions about apparent atrocities by the Israelis. He is the person identified by other officials to me as Israel’s lawyer. He is a player in so many policies, and it’s interesting and kind of surreal to see him in his book pretend he was only part of the ceasefire and hostage diplomacy. That is absolutely not the case. He was a major player in the questioning of the data that humanitarian experts pushed up the chain, repeatedly saying the Palestinians don’t look skinny, sending a chilling effect further down the line. After Trump did win, McGurk was a major factor in the decision not to address new intelligence findings, which I reveal, that suggested both that the Israelis were knowingly committing war crimes and that American officials might be held personally liable for their complicity.

It’s also about emotion. Biden repeatedly described him to people as a “surrogate son.” One fellow official told me they were “a father in search of a son and a son in search of a father.” But there’s a real sympathy and empathy there that, of course, is lacking in talking about Palestinians and Lebanese people.

Was there a moment when Biden could have changed course, but didn’t?

I think the moment is actually in the title. It’s that moment of the World Central Kitchen killings, because it’s a moment of possibility, and then a moment of total failure, and then dishonesty. That’s the moment I see as the moment of maximal possibility, because the evidence is there. Political willingness was there. This is the time at which even Nancy Pelosi is saying, Biden, let’s cut off offensive weapons to Israel. So had the Biden administration wanted to take that shift, they could have. The humanitarian and moral imperative, of course, was there too. And the choice not to do that, and then the choice to work hand-in-gloves with the Israelis to muddy Biden’s own expectations and statements, to me, is the most appalling moment. I don’t know how they could have gone back from there. But I think a phrase that I use and that was used in the New York Times review of McGurk’s book is that the Biden administration effectively became dominated by learned helplessness.

You describe a Washington culture that extends beyond Biden. What do you think people still misunderstand about how these decisions were made?

We have so normalized the imperial presidency in this post-9/11 moment. There’s still a public perception that this really came down to Biden, and he was limited politically because of the election and he had his clear mental decline. I really hope that people get a better understanding of all the kind of D.C. culture and processes that go into enabling atrocities like what happened to Gaza to happen. The fact that there are officials saying, “We’ve all worked together in the Obama administration, we’re working together now, we think in the future we’ll work together, so let’s not rock the boat by identifying a war crime.” The fact that no one questions the clear imbalance of people at the highest levels of the White House meeting with Israeli hostage families at least once or twice a month and never having similar humanizing contact with Palestinian or eventually Lebanese families, including those of American citizens—that’s process. That’s culture.

If you look at that big New York Times story talking about David Milstein, a current aide to Trump’s ambassador in Israel, Mike Huckabee—the story outlines how Milstein changes U.S. government cables to downplay violence against Palestinians. He changes the language that the U.S. government is using internally. I’m so glad that reporting is out there. It also made my stomach drop, because these are the exact patterns we saw from an administration of a different party two years ago, one year ago. These are the patterns that we saw from then–U.S. Ambassador to Israel Jack Lew, and Sonali Korde, then the person at USAID running Gaza policy, downplaying what we were hearing out of Palestinian testimony, effectively not making it a question of the data.

What I hope readers take away from this is that for a more effective and accountable U.S. foreign policy, it’s looking at that whole patchwork of decisions. Not making it just about the fact of who is president.

Public opinion on Israel has shifted considerably. Can the Democratic foreign policy establishment change with it?

I think you see a really interesting attempt by some Democrats to repackage themselves. All of that said, until you address patterns like the administration’s shunting aside congressional oversight of Israel policy, I’m wary that these polls will translate into change. There’s still this real desire in the foreign policy establishment to say: Foreign policy doesn’t matter to voters so we will do what we think is right. That remains the thinking no matter how much voters show that it can be a significant issue. That’s a function of them wanting to retain their influence. It’s also a function of the degree to which they’re captured—whether it’s by corporate interests, or whoever is funding their think tank—their desire to have a revolving-door job in the private sector.

All of that said, it’s a matter of political willingness and courage. Even if we think about who might champion and tap into the public sentiment in office, the question is, can it translate into a lasting public demand for a shift? And, of course, there’s many people for whom a close U.S. relationship with Israel is still deeply important and will remain a priority. Can the shift in public opinion convince those people that change is how we make that relationship both sustainable and morally and strategically appropriate?

Where does Kamala Harris fit into this? You found she was looking at this in a way that Biden wasn’t. Why didn’t she push harder? And could she credibly offer a different policy now?

Kamala Harris, I reveal in the book, was seeing aspects of this that Joe Biden was not. So I write about how she listened to the recording of Hind Rajab, which is just chilling, and it’s so impactful and horrifying. She did say that allowing the Israelis to so-called salami-slice Gaza would be inappropriate and unwise. She was looking at it from moral and strategic angles that I didn’t find Biden did. To me, that makes her inaction and her refusal to outline and endorse different policy changes and steps even more disturbing.

I didn’t find in my reporting that she ever pushed hard in the way that even some members of the Cabinet, or some of Biden’s advisers, did, to talk seriously about cutting off some weapons or pressure the Israelis in other ways. Now, would she have been taken seriously if she had? One senior official said to me she had absolutely no role whatsoever on Gaza. She wasn’t treated as a player on it. Right now, she doesn’t have that record of what she would have done. I expect she will tell us in a future speech. But in my reporting, talking to people who are in touch with her directly, it remains a rhetorical difference that she’s trying to emphasize. And I don’t think that meets the moment of a demand for a policy change that saves lives. Perhaps she’ll offer something more. It’s hard to know right now.

Trump now blames Biden for the bloodshed he inherited. Is that fair?

There are so many factors; Hamas’ choice to initiate this entire period by launching an attack on Oct. 7 and committing what are widely described as war crimes by taking 251 hostages among women, children, and civilians. There are other players—there are Arab and Muslim-majority countries that really chose not to use their influence over Israel as energy suppliers and business and intelligence partners. And of course, there’s a huge level of responsibility that lies with Benjamin Netanyahu and those in his government, and Israeli systems that long predate Oct. 7 that normalized extreme violence toward Palestinians and Lebanese without accountability or change.

Trump said on the campaign trail, Look at the world. There’s so much chaos. So much bloodshed. I will change it. There was a lot of chaos and bloodshed on the Biden administration’s watch, much of it with American fingerprints on it. And I think we have to be honest about that for any hope of breaking out of any of these cycles of violence. To blame it solely on Biden is to obscure Trump’s own responsibility for deeply disproportionate moves on Israel-Palestine during his first presidency, like giving the Israelis much of what they had long wanted without securing any concessions in return for Palestinians. He recognized Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. He shut down the Palestine Liberation Organization mission in Washington. He shut down the American consulate to the Palestinians. He cut off funding for UNRWA. Those are Trump policies. He too, like Biden, had a political coalition ready to support him to change policy on Israel-Palestine and has chosen not to tap that. So I don’t think President Trump can convincingly distance himself from this horror that we see continuing.
news.summary: Kamala Harris’ own role is not what she implies.

news.title: Trump failed to stop inflation. Republicans may pay the price in midterm elections
news.text:
Filling up a basic Ford F-150 truck now costs about $100, up $30 from a year ago. Mortgage rates have jumped to levels that have depressed home sales.

And for the past 12 months, consumer prices have risen faster than paychecks, making the average family poorer.

President Donald Trump would prefer that voters not worry about inflation. But it's hard for them to ignore.

One week before midterm elections that will serve as a referendum on his second term, Trump is struggling to deliver on his campaign promise to bring down costs, even as he insists the country has entered an economic “golden age."

The same frustration that powered his comeback two years ago could now cost Republicans control of Congress.

“Our nation is doing better now than ever before,” Trump insists while campaigning, vowing that interest rates and oil prices will plunge once the war with Iran – which he started – comes to an end.

The word “affordability,” he says, is nothing but “a con job by the Democrats," adding that “it doesn’t mean anything to anybody.”

That rhetoric comes as voters say they're struggling to afford basics like fuel and groceries and as they blame Trump for higher costs, pointing to the Republican president's aggressive tariff policies and the ongoing, unpopular war with Iran.

Record-high diesel prices, in particular, have driven up shipping and farming costs, creating trouble for Republicans in typically conservative states such as Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, where Democrats appear uniquely competitive in races that will shape Trump's final two years in office.

Prices at the pump have become a preeminent issue for voters.

“The costs of things are absolutely the first thing people talk about, but also it’s their pay not keeping up with the cost,” said AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler. “It’s a double whammy.”

"People hate paying more money for gas, and the prices have gone up a lot,” said Stephen Moore, who has previously advised the president on the economy. “It’s frustrating because Trump’s done so many good things for the economy. But with the Iran situation, that’s really had a big effect on the economy, and Republicans may pay a high price for that.”

Misty Reeder, 48, said she considers herself “in the middle” politically but picked all Democrats on her ballot in Easley, South Carolina.

“I’ve noticed that things have been getting a lot harder,” said Reeder, who receives disability payments. “You hear about it everywhere you go."

In the six years that she and her husband have been renting their home, Reeder said their rent had increased by hundreds of dollars.

“Something’s gotta give,” she said. “It’s like a dam — the pressure’s too much, and it’s going to break.”

Sandra Capell, 69, said she wants “to see some change" when it comes to the economy even though she voted Republican in Easley, which is part of South Carolina's conservative Upstate region.

“I think everybody is kind of suffering when it comes to groceries, gas, everything really,” she said. “I’m looking at the Republican Party to jump on the wagon, get in the saddle and let’s bring it back.”

Beti Rosales, 47, said higher prices have taken a toll on her family's Mexican restaurant in Allentown, Pennsylvania, part of the Lehigh Valley that has seesawed between the parties in recent years.

Limes and avocados cost more than before. So does the plumber who's occasionally needed.

Two years ago, Rosales decided to give Trump and Republicans a chance, hoping for relief from inflation.

“The reality now is that it actually didn’t get better," she said. "It actually got worse. The prices of everything have increased."

Rosales is now considering voting Democratic in the midterms. "Maybe fresh new faces might make a difference?” she said.

While running in 2024, Trump hammered President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris, his Democratic opponent in the election, for high inflation, which climbed as high as 9.1% in June 2022. He promised voters he would lower gasoline prices and unlock roaring growth.

“With your vote in this election, I will end inflation,” he vowed.

In less than two years, Trump has aggressively remodeled the U.S. economy. He's slapped double-digit tariffs on many trading partners – including the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico – and sparked trade wars with allies.

The U.S. government now holds stakes in several dozen private companies and he's signed broad income tax cuts into law.

But the persistent challenge of inflation has continued, overshadowing the positives of continued economic growth and a low unemployment rate.

Inflation was 3% when Trump took office and reached 3.7% last month. The president has played down the intensity of inflation, claiming that it is under 2% and “under control.”

Democrats have seized on the discontent, using the same high cost of living that sank them before to pressure vulnerable Republicans and put congressional districts Trump won by even double digits in play.

“Now remember, they promised to lower prices on Day One. Instead, under the failed President Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, stock your fridge, visit the doctor or power your home,” said Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat running for reelection, at a recent rally in Atlanta.

“You work harder and harder, but the treadmill gets faster and steeper and the bills get higher and higher," he told the crowd.

Cait Conley, a Democrat running in New York against Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, one of his party's most vulnerable incumbents, harkened back to his tweet from the last midterm elections, when Biden was president.

Lawler had advised voters to "fill up your tank and go grocery shopping — it will inform your decision.”

In a new ad, Conley said voters should follow that advice this year "and then tell me if the system’s working for you.”

“You deserve better. It shouldn’t be this hard," she says.

Conley and other candidates have pounded on a theme that Democrats believe will be especially effective this cycle: accusing Trump and other Republicans of compounding voters' economic pain by corruptly pursuing policies that help their billionaire donors at the expense of everyday Americans.

“I know you’re frustrated. Washington politicians get rich while you get hurt. Corporations make huge profits while your costs go up," North Carolina Senate candidate Roy Cooper says in an ad airing in the competitive state.

That has included a particular focus on the war with Iran.

“Trump’s war abroad costs taxpayers a billion dollars a day on a war we have no business fighting. Our schools crumble, our factories shutter, our gas prices skyrocket. But when they want war, billion-dollar blank checks," says Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in another spot.

The president "thinks that the economy is doing well because he and his family have enriched themselves to the tune of several billion dollars,” said Amy Richards, 56, a onetime Republican who has voted Democratic since Trump became his party's 2016 nominee.

“He has zero idea what it is like to receive a paycheck and have to feed yourself and your family,” said Richards, standing outside a polling place in her town of Round Rock, Texas, on Friday, "and he doesn’t care.”

Republicans, meanwhile, have tried to cast Democrats as extreme, pointing to an ascendant populist wing that includes a number of Democratic socialists.

Moore, who advised Trump's campaigns, said he wished Republicans would spend more time talking about the economy's strengths, including rising median incomes and a record-setting stock market, even as he acknowledged those numbers might not resonate with voters.

“What matters is how people feel, and clearly people are feeling stressed out financially,” he said.

Some Trump supporters remain satisfied. Renee Blood, 57, an executive assistant in Round Rock, feels the economy has “improved quite well."

“Of course we see gas prices up and down, but things are much more affordable,” she said.

She plans to vote Republican because she worries things will get worse if Democrats return to power.

Trump's golden age might not have arrived, she said, but “we are still working on it.”

news.title: Kamala Harris responds to her critics and Democrats who don’t want her to run again
news.text:
“Nice to meet you, Madam President,” Kamala Harris said, shaking hands with the Coahoma Community College student body representative on her surprise stop by the campus on Thursday afternoon.

Harris likes that disarming joke. She was the biggest political figure to come across this underfunded school in the Mississippi Delta, the grass so dry it crunched as she walked with a gathering of stunned students for a group picture.

“You don’t know how many people this uplifts,” said Don Green, who followed Harris that afternoon from the college to a rural health clinic in Clarksdale, most famous for being the site of the legendary Crossroads of the Blues.

Mike Cavanaugh, a sophomore at the University of Mississippi and president of the campus’ College Democrats, spoke ahead of Harris at a rally that day and answered her questions about voter registration during his brief chat with her on the photo line. “Young people are very excited,” he said.

“It didn’t have to be this way,” is one of the lines Harris used several times on the stump in Mississippi as she campaigned for Democrat Scott Colom, whose challenge to Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is drawing a new burst of national attention and outside money.

“There are so many people who were devastated with the outcome of that election — for good reason, for really good reason,” Harris told CNN backstage before her speech at the rally and two days after her 62nd birthday. “That pain, it lingers, because every day we are witnessing events that we know didn’t have to happen. Could have been different.”

After the interview ended, Harris asked to go back on the record.

“The American people want leaders who aren’t just occupied with looking in the mirror. They want leaders who are looking at the people, you know?” she said. “And they can tell the difference.”

Much of the political insider world has been clear in not wanting Harris to run for president in 2028, or really not wanting to hear from her again, ever. Even before Democrats’ horror year of Joe Biden’s collapse, the contortions over Gaza that she’s still struggling with and Donald Trump’s return, Harris was never good about cultivating donors or keeping aides from fleeing her overly cautious style and the constant infighting that followed.

Yet with her stops in Mississippi and across the country, she’s hearing from many Democratic campaigns who believe having her around helps — and lots of voters who are turning out to show they agree. All told, she’ll end the midterms with more campaign appearances than Barack Obama, and after a late flurry that includes Wisconsin and Georgia this week, more than almost any potential top-tier 2028 candidate.

Several close to the former vice president and 2024 presidential nominee told CNN they believe when she keeps saying she’s thinking about running again, what that means is that after months of soaking up the superfans who bought tickets to her book tour, she hasn’t ruled it out.

But not killing the option is different from pursuing it, whether lining up staff or crafting a new agenda, and Harris acknowledged that her time-treading answers about not having made up her mind can only go on so long. But asked if that means six months or even a year, she said, “I don’t know.”

“I go back and forth. I honestly go back and forth,” Harris said of which way she’s leaning. “There’s so many factors.”

What Harris does know, two years after losing, is that she’s less interested in the game of inches that presidential primaries tend to be.

“I’ll be very specific,” she said. “If I run, my motivation is not to beat other Democrats. It’s to actually do the job.”

Privately, she’s been known to do her wry stare at comments from other Democrats who say she shouldn’t run – convenient, she says, since that would mean they didn’t have to run against her.

“I’m sure there are many who think that I should just sit at home and eat bonbons and cook Doug’s favorite foods,” she said, brushing off the Wall Street Journal article reporting that her husband, Doug Emhoff, had privately told some people that he preferred she didn’t run. “I could cook Doug’s favorite foods and do this.”

Harris said Emhoff was upset at his feelings being portrayed inaccurately. According to one person who has spoken directly with him, his more precise feeling is that the moves the two of them have been making were not done with a plan to run again.

“I feel so strongly and therefore am compelled, and maybe propelled, into doing this, because I know that I can help,” she added. “And how can I sit at home in the comfort of my home when I know there are things I can do to help? I don’t know any other life but that – that’s my point. I don’t know any life that is not about, ‘There’s a problem, what can I do to fix it?’”

Other Democrats could start campaigns in the next several weeks

When Harris talks about “turning pain into purpose,” that means one thing to frustrated voters in the final days of these midterm campaigns, like the retired plumber who shouted “You told us so!” as she ripped Trump’s record in the gym at Columbus High School.

It can mean another to the woman who was herself the candidate Trump beat, even as she kept up the smiles pouring drinks behind the bar at another stop in New Hampshire on Saturday. Around this time two years ago, Harris was calling around to make sure old friends would be with her to celebrate back on the quad at Howard University. She stopped her remarks on Thursday to call back to the man, “Yes, brother, I did.”

Harris did not, like Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, hit the Hamptons fundraising circuit this summer. She has not, as had been proposed in an internal memo circulated among her advisers, launched an extensive engagement tour championing Black voting rights in the wake of the Supreme Court’s Callais decision.

She spent much of the last year on an extended book tour that took her to 27 states and made her millions more than expected. She sold one of the X accounts she controlled to a partnership that netted her more money.

Yet she kept working the phones, whether calling a range of advocates and asking what she could have done differently in her abbreviated presidential run, or checking in with candidates like Texas Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico, to whom she offered some advice over how to manage the ongoing criticism from his former primary opponent, Rep. Jasmine Crockett, whom she endorsed before he won.

Her prospective opponents aren’t waiting on her.

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear has discussed a plan to launch his campaign shortly after the December meeting of the Democratic Governors Association, when he’ll officially wrap up his stint as its chair. After months of public denials while maintaining a national travel schedule, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore has started telling people that after November he’s going to take another look at running for president.

Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg have been all over the country stumping for candidates, including in early states, as aides make sure to remind reporters each time they add more stops. New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker has quietly banked $20 million and started thinking through a South Carolina and Super Tuesday-focused strategy.

Operatives associated with multiple likely contenders are assembling opposition research files on expected opponents and asking around for suggestions of staff to hire. Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, her former running mate, is already saying his advice for the future of the Democratic Party is “pick Pete Buttigieg” (which Harris said she hadn’t seen).

Harris’ motorcade is now just two cars, no sirens. She flies commercial. She pays for staff and security out of the limited fundraising she’s still doing off her old campaign email list, which left her and advisers having to pick between stops she was asked to make and forcing her to stack several virtual appearances into a day she’ll spend this week holed up in a hotel room with a computer instead.

“I have more access, you know? It’s like, the bubble is smaller, and that’s nice. Or there’s not a bubble,” she said.

As for candidates like Rob Sand, running for governor in Iowa, or Adam Hamilton, running for Senate in Kansas, who’ve said they don’t want her to come, Harris says she doesn’t take that personally.

“Oh, I want them to do whatever they need to do to win. I mean that sincerely,” Harris told CNN. “I have run for local, state, and national office. I am not naïve. And I want to win, and I respect whatever decisions they need to make in order to do that.”

Nor was she interested in drawing a line against candidates like Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Florida who said she joined the Democratic Socialists of America specifically as part of launching her campaign, and who will be part of one of Harris’s virtual events this week.

Asked how big of a role the DSA should have in Democrats’ future, Harris said, “We are, as we say, a big tent, and I don’t think anybody should be kicked out.”

The lessons of Mississippi

Mississippi won’t be an early stop on the 2028 presidential calendar. But its electorate could offer a preview of what might await Harris in South Carolina, which is set to host the first Democratic primary again and where Black voters are critical.

“The conventional wisdom,” she said in Mississippi, is, “‘Those are red states, we can’t win there, therefore we won’t go there,’ as opposed to reconditioning ourselves to think about the fact that there are a lot of people who live here who actually care about the things we care about and deserve to be heard and deserve to have us spend our time and resources sitting with them and listening to them.”

Harris first connected with Colom in January, after Rep. Bennie Thompson, the lone Democrat sent to Washington from Mississippi, got them on the phone when she brought her book tour to Jackson. Colom’s campaign to unseat Hyde-Smith, in a state Harris lost to Trump by 23 points, has drawn increasing buzz and now outside spending from both Democratic- and GOP-aligned groups.

Still several Colom consultants initially opposed having Harris join campaign events, worried about nationalizing the race and bringing in a candidate known for losing. With some encouragement, Colom overruled them and called her directly to ask.

Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, who told CNN that he’s considering a presidential run and for months was a main engine of getting Democrats to focus on Colom’s race, drew 100 people when he came to the state two weeks ago. Harris had over 1,000 on their feet in the gym, with an RSVP list that had to be closed because of the fire marshal – even after a sudden decision to bar holding the event at a local college forced a last-minute venue change.

“In this community, it transcends the fact that she lost the last election,” Thompson told CNN while waiting for her to arrive at the community college.

Black maternal mortality was a top issue for Harris when she was vice president. But when he’s campaigning with a focus on 400,000 people in the state without health insurance, rural hospitals closing and mothers dying waiting for a limited number of ambulances to be able to get them, Colom said he saw enormous value having Harris help draw a dozen reporters from across the state to a maternal health care clinic that’s struggling to cover costs.

“The question is: why does Vice President Harris care more about healthcare in our hospitals than our junior senator? If she cares more than our junior senator, I want to bring attention to that issue because that matters,” Colom told CNN after the rally. “You see how many people showed up, you see the excitement. People care about folks that are going to fight for the people.”

In Mississippi, as in Harris’ other stops, the memory of her loss cuts two ways.

“There’s people that think that she got the raw end of the deal,” said Chris Miller, the former chair of the Clark County Democrats in Nevada, who was an early supporter of her 2020 presidential campaign and attended the rally she did with the powerful Culinary Workers Union on behalf of her longtime supporter, state Attorney General Aaron Ford, running for governor. “There’s a feeling that if she wants to run, she should run.”

Patrick Gaspard, who was Obama’s first political director at the White House and has recently been informally advising a number of rising new voices in the Democratic Party including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, was part of the Colom kitchen cabinet encouraging him to bring Harris in.

Videoing the crowd’s reaction to her on stage on his iPhone in Columbus on Thursday night, Gaspard said that has to be factored into any 2028 math, especially at a moment when voters around the country are making clear that they feel abandoned by the people who read tipsheets in green rooms.

“When Muhammad Ali was trying to regain the heavyweight crown, there were a lot of people who were saying they didn’t want him fighting again, they didn’t want him in the ring,” Gaspard told CNN. “They were saying that not because they were worried that Muhammad Ali would fall flat on his face — they were worried he would win.”

news.title: Brazil’s Lula completes stunning turnaround to secure election victory
news.text:
By Alessandra Freitas, CNN

(CNN) — Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was reelected to a historic fourth term Sunday, but his defeated rival and Trump ally Senator Flávio Bolsonaro said he would not accept the results and would mount a legal challenge.

The 80-year-old leftist leader won more than 51% of votes, securing a runoff victory that bucks a broader rightward political shift across Latin America and comes after a campaign dominated by concerns over the cost of living, crime and corruption.

Bolsonaro, who trailed Lula by about 4.4 million votes, said his team would challenge the result after the Supreme Court’s last-minute ruling to extend voting by two hours.

“It is impossible to recognize the election result given how these events unfolded,” Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital Brasilia after Lula’s victory was declared.

“We will take legal action. We will ask for this election to be annulled.”

The vote marks the first time since the return of direct presidential elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the presidency after finishing second in the first round.

“I can assure you that we are going to change the way we govern this country. We are going to give the people a greater role in our decisions,” Lula said after his reelection.

Lula thanked the Brazilian people for their “generosity,” especially the country’s youth who “took to the streets to defend democracy.”

In Rio de Janeiro, Lula’s supporters were seen hugging, beeping their car horns and raising the “L” sign. And in Belo Horizonte, capital of the key swing state Minas Gerais, supporters could be seen chanting and singing following Lula’s victory.

Lula’s win is a major setback for the Bolsonaro political movement, with Flávio failing to accomplish what his father, imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, also couldn’t to do in 2022: defeat Lula at the ballot box.

But the results came after a turbulent election day, with voting being extended by two hours following last-minute pleas from both candidates to electoral authorities.

Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin granted a request from Lula’s campaign, which asked for an extension citing “incidents” affecting buses that provide transportation to polling venues in several states.

Bolsonaro’s campaign had also requested an extension in some areas, citing difficulties voters faced reaching polling stations because of heavy rain. The extension order came around 5 p.m. in Brasilia, just as polls were scheduled to be closing, and many stations had already shut down.

It is unclear how successful Bolsonaro’s challenge of the results will be.

Paulo Sotero, of the Brazil Institute at the Wilson Center, told CNN that the voting extension “was not an irregularity.”

“It was authorized by the Supreme Court of Brazil because there were some localized problems,” Sotero said, adding that Bolsonaro’s “chances of winning a recount or having a new election are very very slim.”

“The Senator has very little space to contest the elections. I think this is a done deal,” he said.

The election outcome will have repercussions beyond Brazil, keeping Latin America’s largest country on a more independent foreign-policy path under Lula, who has emphasized Brazil’s sovereignty and closer ties with the Global South and China amid tensions with the US administration.

Before polls closed on Sunday, US President Donald Trump said that he was “monitoring” Brazil’s presidential runoff. Although he declined to endorse either candidate, he previously praised Flávio’s first-round performance and described the election as “very important.”

Here’s what to know about Sunday’s high-stakes election:

A first-round upset for Lula

According to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, Bolsonaro secured 2.2 million votes more than Lula in the first round of voting. Neither candidate reached the majority needed to win outright, forcing both campaigns to compete for a shrinking pool of undecided voters while trying to mobilize their supporters in a country deeply divided over its political future.

The result exposed vulnerabilities in Lula’s reelection bid, from frustration over the cost of living and crime to difficulties mobilizing parts of his traditional base. It also showed that Jair Bolsonaro’s movement remained strong, even as the former president served a prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 defeat.

The shift in the first round of the election reflected a broader electoral trend across Latin America, where several presidential elections since April 2025 — in Ecuador, Bolivia, Honduras, Chile, Costa Rica, Colombia and Peru — have resulted in victories for right-wing or center-right candidates.

A July Datafolha survey found 44% of Brazilians leaning right or center-right in their political values, compared with 39% on the left or center-left, reversing the balance measured in 2022.

Despite this, leftist Lula prevailed in the second round.

Crime, the economy and last-minute shifts

Public safety emerged as one of the defining issues of the election. A September Quaest/Pax survey found that 28% of Brazilians saw violence as the country’s biggest problem, followed by corruption at 22% and the economy at 19%.

Bolsonaro promised to designate major criminal factions as terrorist groups, expand prisons and lower the age of criminal responsibility. “Those who think I’m radical on public security haven’t seen anything yet,” he said October 13, adding that even El Salvador’s infamous hardline approach under President Nayib Bukele was not enough.

Lula struggled to reconcile his party’s traditional positions with demands for tougher action. A widely circulated clip of him saying last year that drug traffickers were also victims of drug users reinforced what Brian Winter, editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly, called a “longstanding perception that the Brazilian left is soft on crime.” Lula later acknowledged that he had expressed himself poorly.

Lula faced criticism about the state of the economy and affordability. Duringhis first two terms, a commodities boom helped lift millions of Brazilians out of poverty and into the middle class.

This time, many voters had said they felt little progress. Lula can point to low unemployment and easing inflation, but those indicators had not changed perceptions forhouseholds struggling with everyday prices.

Winter compared the dynamic to the 2024 US presidential election, when favorable statistics failed to overcome frustration with prices under President Joe Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris.

Still, many voters have remained loyal to Lula because of the social gains made during his first two terms, while fearing that a Bolsonaro presidency could roll back social rights. Flávio sought to counter those concerns by distancing himself from some traditionally conservative positions.

Part of the shift to the right in Brazil is due to the association of the left with corruption, although scandals have shadowed both campaigns. During last Sunday’s debate, Lula challenged Bolsonaro to open his financial records and pressed him over his ties to Daniel Vorcaro, the former head of the collapsed Banco Master, whose alleged connections to powerful figures have embroiled Brazil’s political and judicial establishment, including the Supreme Court. Flávio, meanwhile, accused Lula of corruption and raised allegations involving the president’s eldest son, known as Lulinha. Lula’s previous corruption convictions were annulled in 2021.

The corruption allegations are deepening political fatiguein Brazil, say experts.“It reinforces the disgust and apathy that Brazilians feel with their political system as a whole,” Winter told CNN.

Women and religion: two crucial divides

But if there was one key group the candidates needed to win over, both experts and campaigns agreed it was women.

Women account for nearly 53% of registered voters and had been more resistant to Bolsonaro-aligned candidates than men. An Oct. 15 Datafolha survey put Lula ahead among women by 49% to 40%, while Flávio led among men by 52% to 40%.

Malu Gatto, an associate professor of Latin American politics at University College London, said the gender gap widened after Jair Bolsonaro emerged in 2018, as men gravitated toward the right and women became more supportive of the Workers’ Party.

Both campaigns addressed violence against women, particularly femicide, after several brutal cases drew national attention. Brazil recorded 1,571 femicides in 2025, the highest number since the crime was defined in law in 2015, according to the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.

According to Gatto, the right traditionally emphasizes tougher criminal penalties for aggressors, while the left places greater emphasis on protection and support for victims, including shelters and specialized services.

Evangelicals, a growing demographic in the predominately Catholic country, have also turned into an important voting bloc for the right. Datafolha found Bolsonaro leading among evangelicals by 62% to 29%, while Lula led among Catholics by 52% to 42%.

Beyond Brazil

Trump praised Flávio Bolsonaro’s electoral performance following the first round but stopped short of formally endorsing him, even as his administration’s tariffs on Brazil and pressure over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution have strained relations with Lula.

The tensions surfaced again during last week’s TV debate. Lula accused the Bolsonaro family of aligning itself with US interests at Brazil’s expense, while Flávio rejected the charge and criticized Lula’s foreign policy.

A Bolsonaro victory could have brought Latin America’s largest economy closer to the US, particularly on security and organized crime, and strengthen a wave of conservative governments elected across the region. Lula has instead emphasized multilateralism, ties with the Global South and China — Brazil’s largest export market — and his resistance to Trump’s tariff measures as a defense of national sovereignty.

The narrow result could also test the country’s stability after Jair Bolsonaro’s attempts to overturn his 2022 defeat led to theJanuary 8, 2023, attacks on government institutions. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.

Lula has secured an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil’s president, but with a more conservative Congress and a razor-thin margin of victory, he faces governing a country that remains deeply divided.

Helen Regan contributed reporting.
