news.title: Gen Z has buyer’s remorse on Trump
news.text:
If there is a Democratic wave in next week’s midterm elections, one of the biggest reasons for that will be young voters.
While voters of all ages have soured on President Donald Trump and the Republican Party since his 2024 victory, polls show that the decline has been particularly pronounced among the young people who’d backed him in surprising numbers just two years ago. That election result prompted endless conversation about a “vibe shift” among Gen Z, and whether younger voters had turned against “woke” progressives, become radicalized by “manosphere” podcasts and TikTok algorithms, or lashed out against Biden-era gerontocracy.
But the story looks very different heading into November. A Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month found that, of people aged 19–34 who voted for Trump over Kamala Harris, only 49 percent approve of his job performance as president. (In contrast, among Trump 2024 voters aged 50 and above, about 75 percent still approve of him.)
Pew also found earlier this year that partisan identification among young adults has shifted — or, rather, reverted. 
In 2022 and 2023, Democrats had a 17-point advantage among adults aged 18–29 — 55 percent of them said they were Democrats or leaned toward Democrats, while just 38 percent said they were Republican or leaned toward the GOP.
In 2024, that gap closed, and Republicans actually took a slight edge, 47 percent to Democrats’ 46 percent. But now, in 2026, Democrats are back to a 16-point advantage, getting 54 percent of young voters compared to the GOP’s 38 percent.
[Media: https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BKjxN/1/]
And it isn’t just that fewer young people are saying they’re Republican. Those who remain Republican are also saying they’re less likely to vote this year.
According to the Harvard Youth Poll released last week, 50 percent of Democrats aged 18–29 say they’ll definitely vote, but only 34 percent of Republicans in that age range say the same. That’s a 16-point partisan gap; the biggest this poll found in recent midterm cycles.
The core reasons for all this in a sense aren’t too surprising. Like older voters, young voters say they’re most concerned about issues like the cost of living, corruption in government, overseas wars, and the cost of health care.
But the swings — and the feelings of betrayal and disappointment among prior Trump supporters — have been particularly dramatic among the young, which raises the question of what about their experience and outlook is influencing their politics in particular. 
To answer that, I spoke to advocates and political consultants focused on young voters. Here’s what they see as the origins — and limits — of the coming youthquake.
How to think about the Gen Z “Trump regretters”
Rachel Janfaza, founder of the Gen Z-focused strategy firm The Up and Up, told me that we should think about young people who voted for Trump in 2024 as really three separate cohorts.
First, she said, are the “hardcore MAGA young people who still stand by the president, just like the older MAGA folks.” They supported him in 2024, and they still do.
Second, she said, are the young people who “are very much on the America First train” but who “resent the fact that Trump’s basically become part of the establishment, whether it comes to building a White House ballroom, or the Epstein files, or starting new wars” — and have moved away from him as a result.
These young people are much less likely to move toward Democrats, but many of them could be disillusioned and not bother to vote this year.
Third, she said, is “a large cohort of young people, predominantly young men, who were never hardcore MAGA, but who voted for Trump in 2024 because they were frustrated by the political conversation at large.” 
“They were frustrated by their economic situation; they were tired of political correctness and the pendulum swinging too far in the direction of ‘wokeness,’” Janfaza continued. These people, she said, now feel “politically homeless.”
Tina Tang of the Democratic-aligned firm Navigator Research has conducted many focus groups interviewing young people who now regret voting for Trump. She told me that many of those “Trump regretters” said they’d initially hoped he would bring change to the political system generally, and that he’d deliver on his promises about the economy and jobs. 
“Young voters are especially worried about jobs right now,” Tang said. “That was actually one of the biggest frustrations we heard from young voters this time around: frustration with the job market. We hear a lot about how he promised a lot of things; he promised the economy was going to get better, that costs were going to come down, that there would be more jobs.”
Young people are pragmatists. They’re losing faith in the system because they think it isn’t delivering.
Several of those I interviewed also urged caution about the common trope that young people tend to be strongly progressive or liberal, a longtime assumption that led many observers to be caught off guard by their swing toward Republicans in 2024.
Indeed, the Harvard Youth poll released this week found that 25 percent of 18- to 29-year-olds thought of themselves as liberal, 23 percent as conservative, and about 46 percent as something in between.
[Media: https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/KJ8eB/1/]
Santiago Mayer, founder of the progressive youth-focused group Voters of Tomorrow, told me that while Gen Z voters often have liberal values and policy views, they often didn’t define politics in ideological terms: “I think for a lot of things many of us would consider progressive, for them, they are common sense, and they’re not necessarily analyzing these issues through a political lens.”
Indeed, Mayer said that while the politicians who are most appealing to young voters can vary in ideology, “the one thing they have in common is that they are very pragmatic and very practical. They are talking about how they’re going to improve things today and how they’re actually going to create material, tangible change in young people’s lives.”
Tang of Navigator Research concurred, telling me that young people are “absolutely still very skeptical of both parties.” She added: “What we hear from young people a lot is: they want to see results.”
And the results they crave are, above all, about the economy and cost of living. Janfaza told me that there’s been a longtime misconception among pundits that young voters are obsessed with identity and the culture war — but, she argues, that was never quite true, and it’s even less true now.
“Now, climate and abortion do not even make it into the top issues that young people are saying they care about,” Janfaza said. “And it doesn’t mean that they don’t care about those issues, but the economic concern just ranks much higher.”
Indeed, she believes that the “flirtation with socialism” among some young voters is really more about policies such as affordable housing, affordable health care, and affordable education — as well as a promise to break with the status quo. “That’s really what young people are hungry for.” 
Key to young people’s worldview is that they’re feeling increasingly pessimistic about that status quo. One striking finding in the Harvard Youth Poll was that, when asked whether they expected to be financially better or worse off than their parents when they reach their age, more said worse — a first-time finding for the poll.
“I think you see that in the numbers that there’s a level of nihilism amongst young voters,” Mayer said. “They’re basically giving Democrats another chance. But I worry that this is kind of our last chance to get them to believe in democracy.” 
And, he worried, if Democrats don’t deliver actual improvements to their lives, “they’ll be gone for good.”

news.title: In Iowa, the Future of American Politics Is Happening Right Now
news.text:
There will be a time soon when Donald Trump is a historic figure and the 20th century is an increasingly hazy memory. If you want to know what that next era of politics will look like, you don’t have to wait. You can go to Iowa, where the gubernatorial election is a window into the future of politics for decades to come.

The millennial-on-millennial contest between Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn is one of the country’s most competitive, despite taking place in what was once a prototypical swing state but has shifted hard toward the GOP in the past decade. Public polls have consistently shown Sand leading—even Lahn acknowledged to reporters that “I think we’re probably down because of the midterm headwinds”—but no one in Iowa politics from either party expects either candidate to win handily. After all, there’s concern about the accuracy of polling in the state where Ann Selzer, its top pollster, showed Kamala Harris winning on the eve of the 2024 election. Trump won by 13 percent, and Selzer, who previously had a stellar track record in polling, promptly retired.

But regardless of who wins, this race is a preview of what the 2030s and 2040s will look like. Sand has tapped into the Democratic resentment toward all politics as usual, Lahn is working toward a synthesis of the populist impulses of Trumpism and the conservative ideology that came before it. It’s a sneak peek of a time when millennials will dominate our politics and the political divides that have dominated since the baby boomers came of age will become increasingly obsolete.

Politics has long been oriented along the battle lines of a prosperous, optimistic United States that was successfully fighting communism abroad and consistently producing economic prosperity at home. That’s not the world of today. Both Sand and Lahn entered the job market at the time of the Great Recession and are now trying to appeal to an Iowa electorate that has long since been ravaged by deindustrialization—and is currently trying to cope with potential dislocations from A.I. It is a world in which print newspapers are increasingly an anachronism and voters get their information from social media. It is a world that has already seen the rise of unconventional politicians ranging from Donald Trump to Zohran Mamdani and is likely to even further depart from the norms of the late 20th century moving forward.

After spending a week traveling across Iowa, talking to voters and following both gubernatorial candidates, I think it’s clear how quickly that era is approaching.

Rob Sand was long considered the star of the Iowa Democratic Party’s bench, but by the time this election cycle started, he wasn’t just the star of the bench; he was the only one there.

Races in Iowa hadn’t been that close recently. It wasn’t just that Trump won handily in 2024 but that incumbent Gov. Kim Reynolds won by nearly 20 points in 2022 as the last Democrat in Iowa’s congressional delegation lost, along with the Democratic state attorney general and state treasurer, who each had spent 40 years in office. The only statewide Democrat left was Sand, who won reelection as state auditor by just under 3,000 votes, in part because of a strenuous work ethic that included an annual tour of all 99 counties in the Hawkeye State.

Sand has long cultivated a moderate image and played up pursuits like his love of hunting and predilection for gas station breakfast pizza. A lanky 44-year-old who painted himself as an earnest advocate for taxpayer efficiency, Sand has tried to conjure up a public perception as half Atticus Finch, half youth pastor. At a visit to a food bank, he earnestly, and without prompting, shares with the volunteers his thoughts on how they can best make peanut butter and jelly sandwiches (peanut butter on both sides of the bread, jelly in between).

On the stump, Sand espouses what even he acknowledges is anti-politics, a deep disdain for the two-party system and American political institutions in general. It’s an nonideological message that harks back to Jimmy Carter as much as any modern politician. Just as Carter was a reaction to a country reeling from Watergate, Sand has an approach that appeals not just to Republicans jaded by Trump and a decade of GOP dominance in Iowa but to Democrats scornful of a political establishment that has allowed Trump and a decade of GOP dominance to happen. His events are studded with signs featuring his campaign slogan: Not redder or bluer, but better and truer.”

Speaking to a crowd at Grinnell College, the elite liberal arts institution located in a small pocket of white-collar prosperity in central Iowa, Sand gave a withering critique of modern American politics. “Does anybody here think that politics is just peachy these days? No.

“Does anybody here think that either the Democratic or the Republican Party, the leadership of either, there are a bunch of heroes that are just doing a bang-up job of solving all of our problems?

“The idea itself is kind of laughable, isn’t it?”

For Sand, both parties consisted of a failed duopoly. “We have two private clubs who are more interested in beating up on each other than they are in actually solving ordinary people’s problems or making ordinary people’s lives better.”

He added, “In fact, a lot of times they are perfectly willing to use ordinary people in order to maintain power by making some group of ordinary people scared of some other, usually smaller group of ordinary people, right? And if they can exploit that fear enough, then they and their friends can pick the pockets of ordinary people while maintaining power. Does anybody think that that’s an unfair description of politics today?” There was no dissent.

This resentment of the “political establishment” has increasingly become de rigueur in a Democratic Party where candidates often compete in their disdain for traditional party institutions. Among the party’s most popular figures are Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who first rose to fame by successfully primarying a member of House Democratic leadership, and Bernie Sanders, who is not even a Democrat. Yet while both Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders are on the left of the party, this disdain is nonideological, as Democrats across the ideological spectrum increasingly disapprove of party leadership. The anti-leadership frustration is perhaps to be expected, given that the status quo has led to two terms of Donald Trump. It’s also resonating on the stump.

Sand was standing on a campus that had long been a die-hard stronghold for progressive Democrats. But as he held forth about the failures of both parties, students in the room nodded their heads in unison.

Speaking to Slate, Sand insisted he disdained the party system despite the fact that he not only was a two-time statewide elected official as a Democrat but had worked on Democratic campaigns in his youth. “I registered as an independent when I first registered to vote because I don’t really like either political party. That doesn’t mean that you’re not active in it,” he said. “Even though I’ve been a participant in the two-party system, I’m still someone that has always looked at it and said, like, why? Why do we do it this way? Doesn’t make any sense. And so, I just think that people appreciate that. And if it’s the right attitude for the moment, great. But I would be talking about it even if it wasn’t.”

Some of Sand’s approach is tailored to his red-state run. Indeed, even as he runs for governor as a Democrat, he’s playing up what he expects would be checks on his own power. He has long buffeted his appeal to independents and Republicans by noting that Iowa’s huge Republican legislative majorities mean it is beyond unlikely that Democrats will gain control of one, let alone both legislative chambers in Des Moines. He didn’t even seem to want a scenario in which Democrats would win a majority when asked by Slate. “I genuinely believe that most of the good stuff is in divided control,” he said. “What an ideal would be is if you had both chambers with razor-thin majorities, where you actually could have people go one way or the other.”

Sand may go further than most Democrats in his seeming indifference as to whether his own party wins legislative majorities in the Hawkeye State, but this is an indication of an aversion to traditional politics that is becoming stronger within the Democratic Party.

It’s not just that the party is perceived to be a failure by many of its voters; it’s that it is actively loathed by a good portion of its membership. The belief that the party has become an empty vessel is one of the rare articles of faith shared across ideological factions. The institutions that were the base of the Democratic Party, like trade unions and Black churches, are shrinking and leaving nothing to replace them except the corrosive nature of social media.

Instead, Sand offers his own simple solutions, a world where we put away our phones—he describes social media as “the scourge of our times: It’s shortening our attention spans, it’s filling our heads with lies, and it’s making us hate people we love”—and just sit down, have coffee with each other, and find common-sense answers to our problems.

On policy, Sand sticks carefully to the center. He opposes transgender athletes competing in women’s sports and focuses his opposition on a controversial school voucher program recently introduced in the state, noting the wasteful spending it entails, as well as what he considers the unneeded subsidies it provides for well-off Iowans.

He even dodges on whether he backs a constitutional amendment on the ballot, backed by Republicans, that would require legislative supermajorities to ever raise personal or corporate income taxes in the future. “Now, making it harder to raise taxes on ordinary people, to me, sounds like a good idea, but I don’t know why they’re including making it harder to raise taxes on corporations at the same time,” he told a crowd in a coffee shop in Davenport, Iowa.

Instead, he focuses on issues like water quality, a topic that has become central in a state where the cancer rate is skyrocketing and many people have become reluctant to drink the tap water, and pushes for systematic reforms to electoral politics, like nonpartisan primaries and term and age limits for elected officials.

This attitude even appealed to attendees at a debate watch party that the Sand campaign held in Davenport for the first gubernatorial debate in early October. It was a crowd of Democratic faithful where local candidates pressed the flesh and attendees sitting down next to each other compared notes on what they did at the John Deere factory in the blue-collar river town.

Alan Lavine, of Bettendorf, told Slate that he liked Sand’s “distrust of the two-party system. I like that he talks about that. It’s one of the main things that I like.” Lavine was a partisan Democrat but was hesitant to say whether he’d show up for a debate party for Josh Turek, the party’s Senate nominee, who was running a more traditional campaign in a toss-up race.

Republicans disdain Sand as a pious hypocrite who is simply the creation of an overly friendly media and his wife’s family wealth. After all, his wife comes from one of the wealthiest families in the state—it has spent eight figures funding his campaign this year—and Sand has long made himself accessible to national reporters. It’s hard to think of a major outlet where the Iowa auditor has not gone on a hunting trip and scarfed down breakfast pizza with a reporter.

If Sand falls short of the governor’s mansion, it’ll be in part because Zach Lahn punctures that aura. But that’s not all the Republican is running on.

Iowa Republican politics had long been defined by a conflict between a powerful establishment and a social conservative opposition that predated Trump. The state’s battle lines don’t cleanly fall along the MAGA–vs.–non-MAGA feuds of other states. Lahn represents neither faction and ran in the primary as a comparative outsider (although he eventually became the anti-establishment favorite as he bested the Trump-endorsed candidate, Congressman Randy Feenstra).

This was helped by the fact that although he is an Iowa native, he had spent much of his adult life living outside the state before returning in 2023 (a fact that Sand has made a key issue of in his campaign, spending millions of dollars to attack his Republican opponent as a carpetbagger from Kansas).

Instead, he represents a deeply Trump-influenced alternative. His politics can be best described as common-good conservatism, a philosophy that represents the explicit use of state power for right-wing ends. The Make America Healthy Again–tinged Lahn sees a real role for the state to achieve conservative goals rather than deferring to the free market. It is the fusionist politics advocated by J.D. Vance when he was in the Senate and still by Sen. Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican. It’s a long, long way from the Reagan-Bush era GOP’s view of economic policy—and represents an evolution even from the second Trump administration.

On the stump, Lahn says the key issue of his campaign is to “protect and preserve the culture of Iowa.” The Republican candidate noted that places like Illinois and Minnesota, particularly Minneapolis, lost this battle to “defend their culture.” There’s no dog whistling here; Lahn has repeatedly been explicit that when he talks about culture, he means one grounded firmly in Christianity. (Unlike many other Republicans fighting the culture war, Lahn doesn’t even bother with the Judeo- prefix when discussing these religious roots of American culture.)

For him, this was under threat by the specter of the left trying to undermine this in the name of “collectivism.” He pointed to the rise of Mamdani in New York and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who he said was “connected directly with the Muslim Brotherhood,” adding, “This is what it looks like when you let down your guard of defending your culture.”

Lahn caveated: “We are a welcoming people. We always have been. Iowa has been a welcoming place, but if you don’t understand what built this country, the ideals that built this country, there’s no way you can defend this country.”

But he also tied culture to fighting powerful private interests as well. Speaking in rural Iowa, he described fighting eminent domain as a cultural issue. “So many of your families in this room came to Iowa probably in 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880. Why did they come here? They didn’t come here for religious freedom, because we already had it in Europe. The Reformation had happened. … What did they not have? They did not have their land. They couldn’t pass something down to their kids. A very small group of wealthy, land-owning, and elite controlled everything.” He added: “By the way, does that sound familiar to how things are going across our country right now in agriculture?”

This leads to Lahn going places that are explicitly against the traditional free-market-based beliefs of the Republican Party of the late 20th century. He scorns what he describes as “market fundamentalism” and told reporters: “We don’t worship the market. Our faith is the foundation of our state.” In particular, one of the targets of his ire has been “unchecked monopolies in the agricultural industry”; he added that, in his view, “monopoly is a failure in the free market.”

Lahn rails against industry consolidation and argues that this was in part what inspired the American Revolution. “The East India Company basically ran England, and [the Founding Fathers] knew what it was like to have an out-of-control monopoly.”

Speaking to Slate, Lahn denounced big business and consolidated power. “Big business buys off both sides. You look at some of the biggest companies; they donate to both sides, and what do they do that for? So we will turn a blind eye. Well, they’re not donating to me,” he insisted.

One example he pointed to was lab-grown meat. “Why is it legal in Iowa? Many states have banned it, but it’s an assault on the cattle industry.

“Who invested $100 million into lab-grown meat? JBS,” Lahn said, taking aim at the Brazilian-based conglomerate that is the largest meatpacking company in the United States. “The people that are processing meat in one of the big three are also in the market of finding other solutions and not working with farmers to undermine farmers.” He added: “And it’s not just them. There’s many of these groups doing it.”

At times Lahn almost sounded like Sand, including when he was asked about the tension of running as an insurgent from the incumbent party. “It’s just that, you know, this has been the most frustrating thing for me running for office, is just that everything is boiled down to this lowest common denominator of: What letter do you have by your name?”

However, he quickly disagreed that there was any commonality. “[Sand] is doing that because he’s just trying to message independents, but he’s not actually trying to solve the problem of politicians being bought off.”

Lahn’s message draws a range of attendees to his events. In Jefferson, Iowa, Tim Heisterkamp was a loyal Republican who voted for Lahn in the primary but was particularly concerned about keeping the state red. “I just don’t think going backwards with the progress that we’ve made in certain areas is worth it. Fiscally, we are as sound as we’ve ever been, and I think we need to keep it that way.” Heisterkamp was also concerned that Sand would roll back the state’s new school voucher program.

In Indianola, Bob Cooper, a bald and bearded attendee, was simply worried about the state of the country. “Muslims are taking over,” he said. “It’s already slipping in now. Like I tell everybody all the time, how do you eat an elephant? One bite at a time, you know. So that’s what’s happened. We’ve accepted this.”

Cooper had not always been a Republican. He grew up in a Democratic family and spent the ’70s as a “hippie” and “not doing much voting.” However, he had come to appreciate that “a lot of good people died so that we can have the freedom that we have. And every day I thank God that I was born in a country where we have freedom. Look at France right now, for instance. The only difference between us and them, we have guns. They don’t have guns.”

Iowa is not likely to be mistaken for France anytime soon, but Lahn’s version of conservatism is still very European. It represents the next step in the transition on the American right in the Trump era to a more populist and more statist worldview. After all, all of Trump’s many heresies from traditional American conservative thought, ranging from his 2016 opposition to entitlement reform to the recent push for the federal government to take ownership stakes in a number of privately owned companies, are far more in tune with the politics of Marine Le Pen than those of Mitt Romney.

There’s no indication that there will be any reversion to the GOP of the past. Instead, in the post-Trump era, Republicans will have to seek to emulate what aspects of Trumpism can actually be copied, as opposed to what are unique to a man who was a celebrity for generations before he was a politician.

Lahn’s effort, which encompasses both a strain of nativism and real skepticism of corporate power along with many traditional shibboleths of the American right, feels the logical next step in this, an attempt to redefine the GOP around the political coalition that reelected Trump in 2024 and move beyond the political landscape of the past.

Of course, the stakes in the race include not just the governor’s mansion and which millennial will be an ideological flag bearer for their party moving forward but potentially a Senate seat. Iowa’s Republican incumbent Chuck Grassley is 93 years old. Although Grassley is in good health and has even filed to run for reelection in 2028, he has noted the risk of being replaced by a Democratic governor if he dies in office. When asked how they would deal with a Grassley replacement, both Sand and Lahn agreed that they would consider voting for a Republican.

Sand said he would look to “trying to pick someone that’s actually going to represent Iowans, not a party. That might be picking someone who’s independent.” The Democratic candidate even noted that he could think of one Republican he would appoint. “I wouldn’t name them because I don’t want them to get kicked out of the party. I could think of at least one that I think would do a good job.”

Lahn pointed to someone who understands “the grassroots.” He added: “You’re going out to Washington, D.C., to fight a machine … the Senate is one place you can actually have a real influence. So I would want somebody that would be willing to take these more populist ideas—economic and health—and carry that on outside of Iowa.”

The governor of Iowa always takes on an outsize role in American politics due to the state’s first-in-the-country caucuses. If Lahn wins, he will be there as a kingmaker in 2028 when Republicans go first. And Sand has already pledged that if he wins, he will ensure that the Iowa law that mandates that the Hawkeye State go first is followed even though the Democratic National Committee has attempted to end Iowa’s status as an early state.

And of course that will just be amplified because of their relative youth and because a win from either would justly be considered impressive. Sand would be the first Democrat elected governor in 20 years in a state that Trump won three times. If Lahn wins, it would be despite being consistently down in polls and outspent.

But what would stand out is how much they would represent the future of their parties. Lahn’s views represent the fusion of Trumpism, inchoate as it may be as an ideology, with the Republican Party of the past. And Sand represents the wholesale rejection among Democrats of party institutions of the past. Although he shares little politically with figures like Zohran Mamdani, there is a commonality in their rejection of their party and efforts to build a politics that rejects the institutions of the past.

And regardless of who wins this matchup this year, it is likely to be an indication of the battle lines drawn in political races for decades to come.
news.summary: Win or lose, these two candidates for governor represent the future of their parties.

news.title: These key Senate races will determine which party controls the body next year
news.text:
Thirty-five Senate seats are up for grabs when Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3. A key handful of them will be critical in determining whether Democrats or Republicans control the chamber next year.

Republicans currently control the Senate with 53 seats. Democrats and two independents make up the Senate minority with 47 seats.

In order for Democrats to take the chamber back, they’ll have to net four seats in the upcoming election. Republicans can afford to lose up to three and still be considered the Senate majority with the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance.

Some of the races that were closely watched earlier this year have slid from the spotlight as the election grew near. Republicans seem to have abandoned efforts to unseat incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia and have pulled out of spending in North Carolina, where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper now seems poised to best former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley to fill retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis' seat.

As both parties prepare for the final leg of the campaign, here are some of the most closely watched Senate races.

Michigan: A bitter fight against a progressive newcomer

 Lean Democrat

Republican nominee Mike Rogers is no stranger to Senate races -- the former congressmen lost his 2024 bid to now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin by less than 20,000 votes.

Rogers is squaring off this time against progressive Abdul El-Sayed, a former health executive who bested a moderate candidate in the Democratic primary.

Republicans have gone to great lengths to frame El-Sayed as “radical" over his support for Medicare for all and his positions on immigration. They've also attacked him for his faith and ethnicity. Rogers has falsely linked him to terrorist groups and President Donald Trump has gone as far as calling him a "vicious, violent jihadist" while urging voters to reject him to "preserve our religion, our values, and our heritage."

El-Sayed, who was born to Egyptian immigrant parents in Rochester Hills, Michigan, has denied ties to terrorism and called those characterizations Islamophobic.

El-Sayed told ABC News Live anchor Linsey Davis last week, "They think they can point to my name and my faith and distract us from the fact that we can't afford our gas and we can't afford our groceries."

Rogers told Davis in a separate interview the he thought he was making inroads with traditionally Democratic Jewish and Black voters who are wary of El-Sayed.

Michigan has voted for Trump in two of the last three elections, yet Democrats have prevailed in every Senate race since 1994.

Texas: A primary upset puts Dems in the hunt

Texans have not been represented by a Democrat in the Senate for 33 years, but Democrats say this could be the year that changes.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton beat long-time incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a costly GOP primary runoff thanks to Trump's late endorsement. Paxton, a hardliner and ally of the president, is seen by many Republicans as a harder sell in the general election than Cornyn would have been.

Paxton has had several scandals in his time in the public eye. He was impeached in 2023 on allegations of abuse of office, bribery and corruption but was acquitted by the state Senate. He was indicted on securities fraud charges in 2015 but reached a pretrial agreement with prosecutors just weeks before trial in which he agreed to community service, legal ethics courses and pay $300,000 in restitution in return for not having to admit guilt.

Democrat James Talarico is a former state representative and Presbyterian seminarian. Republicans have tried to paint the 37-year-old progressive as far-left and radical.

Democrats hope Paxton’s lack of favorability coupled with larger concerns about affordability could be enough to end their three-decade Senate drought.

Republicans are taking no chances, pouring millions into this race and even opted to hold their inaugural midterm convention in Dallas.

The race is the most expensive Senate race in history: Outside groups have contributed more than a quarter-billion dollars to elect Paxton. Over $500 million has been spent on ads in the state, according to AdImpact.

Alaska: 4 candidates, 2 Dan Sullivans

Incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan will square off against former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and another candidate with the same name in another surprisingly close race.

Alaska’s ranked-choice voting sends the top four vote-getters in primaries to the general election. Peltola is advantaged by being the only Democrat to advance.

In addition to Peltola, Sen. Sullivan faces another opponent on the ballot also named Dan Sullivan, an independent, and Republican Gerald Heikes, who made the final four when the fourth-place finisher dropped out.

Republicans, including Trump, have made a point of reminding voters to check that they’re casting their ballot for the “real Dan Sullivan,” and on Oct. 23 he directed the Justice Department to preemptively sue to block certification of the results if the incumbent narrowly loses.

Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024.

Ohio: An appointee senator vs. a former one

The Ohio Senate race features two candidates fighting for their chance to return to the Senate: incumbent Republican John Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his 2024 reelection bid to Bernie Moreno.

Husted was appointed by Ohio GOP Gov. Mike DeWine in 2025 to fill the Senate seat left vacant by Vice President JD Vance. This race will determine who finishes out the remainder of Vance’s term until 2029.

This is Husted’s first time on the statewide ballot. Though Ohio has been moving increasingly toward Republicans in recent elections, Husted faces a tough race amid growing concerns about affordability and data centers in his home state.

Brown lost his reelection bid against newcomer Moreno by about four points in 2024, though he outperformed Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the state. The three-term senator is making a pitch to working-class voters concerned about cost-of-living issues.

Kansas: Challenging the GOP's lock on Senate seat

The Kansas Senate race was not expected to be competitive -- Trump won the state by 16 points in 2024 and Republicans have held both Senate seats in Kansas for nearly a century. Yet even incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall has conceded that it's “quite a close race” this cycle.

Marshall, a medical doctor who served in the House before being elected to the Senate in 2020, has largely supported Trump’s policies during his time in Congress. His opponent, Adam Hamilton, has sought to emphasize Marshall’s ties to the unpopular policies that have created economic challenges for voters.

Hamilton is reverend of the largest United Methodist congregation in the nation. He has tried to brand himself as an “independent-minded” Democrat but Marshall has said Hamilton is “too woke” to represent the people of Kansas.

Maine: Can a 100-day-long campaign unseat an institution?

Longtime Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins has repeatedly defied the odds, and kept her seat even after being counted out. She’s a moderate Republican who has been more willing than most in her party to break with the president on some issues.

But Democrats think Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and majority leader, could put an end to Collins’ nearly-30-year Senate career.

Jackson was a late entry into the race after Graham Platner, the original nominee, dropped out following sexual assault allegations.

Collins, the chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has name recognition and a long record of serving Maine on her side and has tried to highlight her willingness to vote against her party.

Jackson has tried to show Collins failed to when it counted -- notably, Jackson has accused her of "paving the way" for the Supreme Court to overturn Roe v. Wade by casting the deciding vote for Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

Iowa: A surprisingly competitive race

Trump has been rallying in Iowa to support Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson’s bid to replace retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst in a race that few thought would be competitive at the beginning of the cycle.

There are no Democrats in Iowa's congressional delegation and Trump won the state by a commanding 13 points in 2024. Iowa has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.

But rising costs caused by the Iran war have hit Iowa farmers hard. Many see moderate Democratic nominee Josh Turek, a state representative and two-time Paralympics gold medalist in wheelchair basketball, as a formidable candidate against Hinson.
news.summary: As both parties prepare for the final leg of the campaign, here are some of the most closely watched Senate races.
news.author: Allison Pecorin

Thirty-five Senate seats are up for grabs when Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3. A key handful of them will be critical in determining whether Democrats or Republicans control the chamber next year.

Republicans currently control the Senate with 53 seats. Democrats and two independents make up the Senate minority with 47 seats.

In order for Democrats to take the chamber back, they’ll have to net four seats in the upcoming election. Republicans can afford to lose up to three and still be considered the Senate majority with the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance.

Some of the races that were closely watched earlier this year have slid from the spotlight as the election grew near. Republicans seem to have abandoned efforts to unseat incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia and have pulled out of spending in North Carolina, where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper now seems poised to best former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley to fill retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis' seat.

As both parties prepare for the final leg of the campaign, here are some of the most closely watched Senate races.

Michigan: A bitter fight against a progressive newcomer

 Lean Democrat

Republican nominee Mike Rogers is no stranger to Senate races -- the former congressmen lost his 2024 bid to now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin by less than 20,000 votes.

Rogers is squaring off this time against progressive Abdul El-Sayed, a former health executive who bested a moderate candidate in the Democratic primary.

Republicans have gone to great lengths to frame El-Sayed as “radical" over his support for Medicare for all and his positions on immigration. They've also attacked him for his faith and ethnicity. Rogers has falsely linked him to terrorist groups and President Donald Trump has gone as far as calling him a "vicious, violent jihadist" while urging voters to reject him to "preserve our religion, our values, and our heritage."

El-Sayed, who was born to Egyptian immigrant parents in Rochester Hills, Michigan, has denied ties to terrorism and called those characterizations Islamophobic.

El-Sayed told ABC News Live anchor Linsey Davis last week, "They think they can point to my name and my faith and distract us from the fact that we can't afford our gas and we can't afford our groceries."

Rogers told Davis in a separate interview the he thought he was making inroads with traditionally Democratic Jewish and Black voters who are wary of El-Sayed.

Michigan has voted for Trump in two of the last three elections, yet Democrats have prevailed in every Senate race since 1994.

Texas: A primary upset puts Dems in the hunt

Texans have not been represented by a Democrat in the Senate for 33 years, but Democrats say this could be the year that changes.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton beat long-time incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a costly GOP primary runoff thanks to Trump's late endorsement. Paxton, a hardliner and ally of the president, is seen by many Republicans as a harder sell in the general election than Cornyn would have been.

Paxton has had several scandals in his time in the public eye. He was impeached in 2023 on allegations of abuse of office, bribery and corruption but was acquitted by the state Senate. He was indicted on securities fraud charges in 2015 but reached a pretrial agreement with prosecutors just weeks before trial in which he agreed to community service, legal ethics courses and pay $300,000 in restitution in return for not having to admit guilt.

Just weeks before he is scheduled to go to trial on securities fraud charges stemming from theH state indictment filed against him in 2015, Paxton reaches a pretrial agreement with prosecutors to resolve the case. Paxton agrees to complete a series of actions, including doing community service, taking legal ethics courses, and paying nearly $300,000 in restitution. Not required to admit guilt, Paxton releases a statement, saying, "There will never be a conviction in this case nor am I guilty."

Democrat James Talarico is a former state representative and Presbyterian seminarian. Republicans have tried to paint the 37-year-old progressive as far-left and radical.

Democrats hope Paxton’s lack of favorability coupled with larger concerns about affordability could be enough to end their three-decade Senate drought.

Republicans are taking no chances, pouring millions into this race and even opted to hold their inaugural midterm convention in Dallas.

The race is the most expensive Senate race in history: Outside groups have contributed more than a quarter-billion dollars to elect Paxton. Over $500 million has been spent on ads in the state, according to AdImpact.

Alaska: 4 candidates, 2 Dan Sullivans

Incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan will square off against former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and another candidate with the same name in another surprisingly close race.

Alaska’s ranked-choice voting sends the top four vote-getters in primaries to the general election. Peltola is advantaged by being the only Democrat to advance.

In addition to Peltola, Sen. Sullivan faces another opponent on the ballot also named Dan Sullivan, an independent, and Republican Gerald Heikes, who made the final four when the fourth-place finisher dropped out.

Republicans, including Trump, have made a point of reminding voters to check that they’re casting their ballot for the “real Dan Sullivan,” and on Oct. 23 he directed the Justice Department to preemptively sue to block certification of the results if the incumbent narrowly loses.

Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024.

Ohio: An appointee senator vs. a former one

The Ohio Senate race features two candidates fighting for their chance to return to the Senate: incumbent Republican John Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his 2024 re-election bid to Bernie Moreno.

Husted was appointed by Ohio GOP Gov. Mike DeWine in 2025 to fill the Senate seat left vacant by Vice President JD Vance. This race will determine who finishes out the remainder of Vance’s term until 2029.

This is Husted’s first time on the statewide ballot. Though Ohio has been moving increasingly toward Republicans in recent elections, Husted faces a tough race amid growing concerns about affordability and data centers in his home state.

Brown lost his re-election bid against newcomer Moreno by about four points in 2024, though he outperformed Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the state. The three-term senator is making a pitch to working-class voters concerned about cost-of-living issues.

Kansas: Challenging the GOP's lock on Senate seat

The Kansas Senate race was not expected to be competitive -- Trump won the state by 16 points in 2024 and Republicans have held both Senate seats in Kansas for nearly a century. Yet even incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall has conceded that it's “quite a close race” this cycle.

Marshall, a medical doctor who served in the House before being elected to the Senate in 2020, has largely supported Trump’s policies during his time in Congress. His opponent, Adam Hamilton, has sought to emphasize Marshall’s ties to the unpopular policies that have created economic challenges for voters.

Hamilton is reverend of the largest United Methodist congregation in the nation. He’s tried to brand himself as an “independent-minded” Democrat but Marshall has said Hamilton is “too woke” to represent the people of Kansas.

Maine: Can a 100-day-long campaign unseat an institution?

Longtime Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins has repeatedly defied the odds, and kept her seat even after being counted out. She’s a moderate Republican who has been more willing than most in her party to break with the president on some issues.

But Democrats think Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and majority leader, could put an end to Collins’ nearly-30-year Senate career.

Jackson was a late entry into the race after Graham Platner, the original nominee, dropped out following sexual assault allegations.

Collins, the chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has name recognition and a long record of serving Maine on her side and has tried to highlight her willingness to vote against her party.

Jackson has tried to show Collins failed to when it counted -- notably, Jackson has accused her of "paving the way" for the Supreme Court to overturn Roe v. Wade by casting the deciding vote for Justice Brett Kavanaugh.

Iowa: A surprisingly competitive race

Trump has been rallying in Iowa to support Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson’s bid to replace retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst in a race that few would be competitive at the beginning of the cycle.

There are no Democrats in Iowa's congressional delegation and Trump won the state by a commanding 13 points in 2024. Iowa has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.

But rising costs caused by the Iran war have hit Iowa farmers hard. Many see moderate Democratic nominee Josh Turek, a state representative and two-time Paralympics gold medalist in wheelchair basketball, as a formidable candidate against Hinson.

news.title: Brazil’s Lula wins reelection with victory over Trump ally Bolsonaro, who rejects result
news.text:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was reelected to a historic fourth term Sunday, but his defeated rival and Trump ally Senator Flávio Bolsonaro said he would not accept the results and would mount a legal challenge.

The 80-year-old leftist leader won more than 51 percent of votes, securing a runoff victory that bucks a broader rightward political shift across Latin America and comes after a campaign dominated by concerns over the cost of living, crime and corruption.

Bolsonaro, who trailed Lula by about 4.4 million votes, said his team would challenge the result after the Supreme Court’s last-minute ruling to extend voting by two hours.

“It is impossible to recognize the election result given how these events unfolded,” Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital Brasilia after Lula’s victory was declared.

“We will take legal action. We will ask for this election to be annulled.”

The vote marks the first time since the return of direct presidential elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the presidency after finishing second in the first round.

“I can assure you that we are going to change the way we govern this country. We are going to give the people a greater role in our decisions,” Lula said after his reelection.

Lula thanked the Brazilian people for their “generosity,” especially the country’s youth who “took to the streets to defend democracy.”

In Rio de Janeiro, Lula’s supporters were seen hugging, beeping their car horns and raising the “L” sign. And in Belo Horizonte, capital of the key swing state Minas Gerais, supporters could be seen chanting and singing following Lula’s victory.

Lula’s win is a major setback for the Bolsonaro political movement, with Flávio failing to accomplish what his father, imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, also couldn’t to do in 2022: defeat Lula at the ballot box.

But the results came after a turbulent election day, with voting being extended by two hours following last-minute pleas from both candidates to electoral authorities.

Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin granted a request from Lula’s campaign, which asked for an extension citing “incidents” affecting buses that provide transportation to polling venues in several states.

Bolsonaro’s campaign had also requested an extension in some areas, citing difficulties voters faced reaching polling stations because of heavy rain. The extension order came around 5 p.m. in Brasilia, just as polls were scheduled to be closing, and many stations had already shut down.

It is unclear how successful Bolsonaro’s challenge of the results will be.

Paulo Sotero, of the Brazil Institute at the Wilson Center, told CNN that the voting extension “was not an irregularity.”

“It was authorized by the Supreme Court of Brazil because there were some localized problems,” Sotero said, adding that Bolsonaro’s “chances of winning a recount or having a new election are very very slim.”

“The Senator has very little space to contest the elections. I think this is a done deal,” he said.

The election outcome will have repercussions beyond Brazil, keeping Latin America’s largest country on a more independent foreign-policy path under Lula, who has emphasized Brazil’s sovereignty and closer ties with the Global South and China amid tensions with the US administration.

Before polls closed on Sunday, US President Donald Trump said that he was “monitoring” Brazil’s presidential runoff. Although he declined to endorse either candidate, he previously praised Flávio’s first-round performance and described the election as “very important.”

Here’s what to know about Sunday’s high-stakes election:

A first-round upset for Lula

According to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, Bolsonaro secured 2.2 million votes more than Lula in the first round of voting. Neither candidate reached the majority needed to win outright, forcing both campaigns to compete for a shrinking pool of undecided voters while trying to mobilize their supporters in a country deeply divided over its political future.

The result exposed vulnerabilities in Lula’s reelection bid, from frustration over the cost of living and crime to difficulties mobilizing parts of his traditional base. It also showed that Jair Bolsonaro’s movement remained strong, even as the former president served a prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 defeat.

The shift in the first round of the election reflected a broader electoral trend across Latin America, where several presidential elections since April 2025 — in Ecuador, Bolivia, Honduras, Chile, Costa Rica, Colombia and Peru — have resulted in victories for right-wing or center-right candidates.

A July Datafolha survey found 44 percent of Brazilians leaning right or center-right in their political values, compared with 39 percent on the left or center-left, reversing the balance measured in 2022.

Despite this, leftist Lula prevailed in the second round.

Crime, the economy and last-minute shifts

Public safety emerged as one of the defining issues of the election. A September Quaest/Pax survey found that 28 percent of Brazilians saw violence as the country’s biggest problem, followed by corruption at 22 percent and the economy at 19 percent.

Bolsonaro promised to designate major criminal factions as terrorist groups, expand prisons and lower the age of criminal responsibility. “Those who think I’m radical on public security haven’t seen anything yet,” he said October 13, adding that even El Salvador’s infamous hardline approach under President Nayib Bukele was not enough.

Lula struggled to reconcile his party’s traditional positions with demands for tougher action. A widely circulated clip of him saying last year that drug traffickers were also victims of drug users reinforced what Brian Winter, editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly, called a “longstanding perception that the Brazilian left is soft on crime.” Lula later acknowledged that he had expressed himself poorly.

Lula faced criticism about the state of the economy and affordability. During his first two terms, a commodities boom helped lift millions of Brazilians out of poverty and into the middle class.

This time, many voters had said they felt little progress. Lula can point to low unemployment and easing inflation, but those indicators had not changed perceptions for households struggling with everyday prices.

Winter compared the dynamic to the 2024 US presidential election, when favorable statistics failed to overcome frustration with prices under President Joe Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris.

Still, many voters have remained loyal to Lula because of the social gains made during his first two terms, while fearing that a Bolsonaro presidency could roll back social rights. Flávio sought to counter those concerns by distancing himself from some traditionally conservative positions.

Part of the shift to the right in Brazil is due to the association of the left with corruption, although scandals have shadowed both campaigns. During last Sunday’s debate, Lula challenged Bolsonaro to open his financial records and pressed him over his ties to Daniel Vorcaro, the former head of the collapsed Banco Master, whose alleged connections to powerful figures have embroiled Brazil’s political and judicial establishment, including the Supreme Court. Flávio, meanwhile, accused Lula of corruption and raised allegations involving the president’s eldest son, known as Lulinha. Lula’s previous corruption convictions were annulled in 2021.

The corruption allegations are deepening political fatigue in Brazil, say experts. “It reinforces the disgust and apathy that Brazilians feel with their political system as a whole,” Winter told CNN.

Women and religion: two crucial divides

But if there was one key group the candidates needed to win over, both experts and campaigns agreed it was women.

Women account for nearly 53 percent of registered voters and had been more resistant to Bolsonaro-aligned candidates than men. An Oct. 15 Datafolha survey put Lula ahead among women by 49 percent to 40 percent, while Flávio led among men by 52 percent to 40 percent.

Malu Gatto, an associate professor of Latin American politics at University College London, said the gender gap widened after Jair Bolsonaro emerged in 2018, as men gravitated toward the right and women became more supportive of the Workers’ Party.

Both campaigns addressed violence against women, particularly femicide, after several brutal cases drew national attention. Brazil recorded 1,571 femicides in 2025, the highest number since the crime was defined in law in 2015, according to the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.

According to Gatto, the right traditionally emphasizes tougher criminal penalties for aggressors, while the left places greater emphasis on protection and support for victims, including shelters and specialized services.

Evangelicals, a growing demographic in the predominately Catholic country, have also turned into an important voting bloc for the right. Datafolha found Bolsonaro leading among evangelicals by 62 percent to 29 percent, while Lula led among Catholics by 52 percent to 42 percent.

Beyond Brazil

Trump praised Flávio Bolsonaro’s electoral performance following the first round but stopped short of formally endorsing him, even as his administration’s tariffs on Brazil and pressure over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution have strained relations with Lula.

The tensions surfaced again during last week’s TV debate. Lula accused the Bolsonaro family of aligning itself with US interests at Brazil’s expense, while Flávio rejected the charge and criticized Lula’s foreign policy.

A Bolsonaro victory could have brought Latin America’s largest economy closer to the US, particularly on security and organized crime, and strengthen a wave of conservative governments elected across the region. Lula has instead emphasized multilateralism, ties with the Global South and China — Brazil’s largest export market — and his resistance to Trump’s tariff measures as a defense of national sovereignty.

The narrow result could also test the country’s stability after Jair Bolsonaro’s attempts to overturn his 2022 defeat led to the January 8, 2023, attacks on government institutions. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.

Lula has secured an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil’s president, but with a more conservative Congress and a razor-thin margin of victory, he faces governing a country that remains deeply divided.

Helen Regan contributed reporting.

news.title: As Trump endorses Netanyahu ahead of Israel poll, President Herzog says "Trump can't intervene on his discretion"
news.text: Jerusalem [Israel], October 26 (ANI): Israeli President Isaac Herzog has affirmed that any decision on who will lead Israel after Tuesday's election will be taken without any external pressure. Herzog who will be called upon to invite one of the Knesset Members to form a government made the remarks amidst a second endorsement from US President Donald Trump for incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud led coalition. Speaking to US network, MS NOW, Herzog said he would not bow to pressure from President Donald Trump. “I don’t think the President of the United States or anybody else can intervene in my discretion, the discretion has to be based on certain facts, and we will see what the facts are...There will be a lot of pressure, though, regardless,” he said.Herzog said he has “huge respect” for Trump and welcomes any dialogue, but the decision will be his, and his alone.Earlier, Trump endorsed Netanyahu for the second time saying, " When you go to the Polls, please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding Warrior Prime Minister! Israel was called The Little Satan, with the United States being called The Big Satan, by some very evil people. There can no longer be the chant heard around the World of “Death to America, Death to Israel,” and there won’t be. Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started."Netanyahu has since shared the exact post of Donald Trump on his X account. On Sunday, Netanyahu used the endorsement he got from US President Trump to project a doomsday scenario if his coalition does not come to power. Netanyahu posted an AI-generated image on social media depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv, warning the public that voting for anyone other than him could expose Israelis to the danger of a “second Holocaust.”Quoting Right-wing activist Yuval Blumberg's statements, Netanyahu's post read, “The State of Israel is in real and tangible existential danger. If the Iranians acquire nuclear weapons, nothing will ever be the same again. Everything is so trivial compared to the existential threat of Iran and the Shiite axis.""We have another two years of Trump to finish the work in Iran, and there's no telling what will come after that—whether it's Kamala Harris or some other mediocre figure. This is the window of time we have left to complete the necessary work to ensure our physical existence for the coming years. All the required resources of the state must be invested in this mission... This won't happen with a prime minister who can't pick up the phone and have a continuous, intimate conversation with Trump," the post read.His main rival Gadi Eisenkot chose to play down the endorsement saying that Trump would cooperate with any chosen leader of Israel. "Donald Trump is a true friend of Israel. I appreciate his actions and commitment to Israel's security, and I am convinced that he will work in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people. Citizens of Israel, I believe in you that you will choose according to the dictates of your conscience and for the future of the State of Israel. Trust me. Straight! A large gap victory over the Likud will ensure the change and bring about the victory of the majority of the Zionist state-oriented [camp] in Israel," he said.Israel uses a party-list proportional representation system. Under this system, voters cast their ballots for lists of candidates, and each list receives a number of seats in the Knesset proportional to its share of the vote. Israel has an electoral threshold: only lists that receive at least 3.25% of the valid votes participate in the allocation of Knesset seats. The Knesset is made up of 120 Members. (ANI)

news.title: How Project 2025 became the blueprint for Republicans' failure | Opinion
news.text:
Two years ago, as Donald Trump and Kamala Harris were nearing the finish line in the 2024 presidential election, one controversial topic kept coming up during their debates and rallies.

Project 2025.

Harris warned that Project 2025, a 920-page plan to transform the federal government produced by the hard-right Heritage Foundation, would "take our country backward" and "weaken the middle class."

Trump, knowing that polls in 2024 showed a majority of voters did not like Project 2025's projected goals, insisted he had nothing to do with it and even called the plan's authors part of "the radical right."

Guess what happened next.

Trump won a second term as president, hired the people who wrote Project 2025 to run his administration and let them get to work implementing it.

Project 2025 doesn't make as many headlines these days. But the impacts have been felt across the government.

Federal agencies slashed staffing, but then had to rehire some employees. Militarized mass deportations caused havoc in American cities. Trump's team hunted down any reference to "diversity, equity and inclusion" and halted programs addressing LGBTQ+ issues. Energy sector regulations were disabled. Disaster planning funds were washed away.

It's time to remember Project 2025, to look at the context of what it has meant in the first 21 months of Trump's second term. Just ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, it's time to decide whether this is what you want from your government.

Ways Project 2025 was enacted in two years of Republican reign

Project 2025 was a blueprint, but Trump rarely sticks directly to any plan. Consider FEMA, the Federal Emergency Management Agency. Project 2025 proposed pushing more disaster response responsibility onto the states. But Trump had another idea – using FEMA funding as political leverage in blue states.

"One of the most surprising features of this administration has been the outright, unabashed politicization of emergency aid," said William Galston, a senior fellow at The Brookings Institution, a nonpartisan research think tank. "That used to be one of the few remaining areas of genuine neutrality."

Galston and Elaine Kamarck, another Brookings senior fellow, told me Project 2025 allowed Trump's second term to get off to a very quick start but also caused friction as an eagerness to slash federal programs and employment prompted concerns from Cabinet secretaries who saw their agencies and staff impacted.

And they question whether much of what Trump has accomplished with Project 2025 has staying power, because so much of it was implemented by executive orders that the next president can eliminate.

"They're more than happy to have people believe that an executive order is akin to a bold and revolutionary bill signing of something that came out of Congress," Kamarck told me of Trump's team. "And it's just not true."

But the damage of Project 2025 can be lasting, and a political danger for future presidents. One place to look for that is FEMA. Workforce reductions at FEMA and cuts to state grant programs landed just ahead of an unusually calm hurricane season in the Atlantic Ocean.

George W. Bush took sustained criticism in his second term as president for his administration's disaster preparedness and bumbling response in 2005 to Hurricane Katrina, which killed nearly 2,000 people.

Trump should know – the next storm is always out there, somewhere.

"They're just lucky that it hasn't come to bite them in the (expletive). But it will," Kamarck said. "There's no doubt that sometime in the next two to four years there will be some kind of Katrina-level disaster."

Galston told me the next president will need to rebuild FEMA for when that disaster hits because they will take the blame for a bad federal response, even if Trump is the reason the resources and staffing are no longer available.

Your Turn: I thought Trump wouldn't be that bad. I was wrong. | Opinion Forum

Project 2025 proposed, and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency under Elon Musk accomplished, massive cuts to the federal workforce with voluntary incentives to quit. But Kamarck told me we won't really know the scale of the cuts until 2029, because so many of those eliminated positions are now being restored.

DOGE is now a sad joke, a short-term chaos agent that ludicrously claimed to have found $215 billion in savings in federal spending. The Government Accountability Office in August reported that much of that was exaggerated or unproven. Musk in December said that DOGE had been "somewhat successful," but that he would not do it again if he had the chance.

And the cleanup for that chaos continues.

"Nobody quite knows yet how many people they will need to hire back and whether or not people will want to come back to the federal workforce because of the trauma that DOGE inflicted on them," Kamarck said.

Attacking DEI became a staple of Trump's agenda

Project 2025 also exploited political culture war issues to attack at the federal level programs as varied as diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) in hiring to reliance on fossil fuels versus renewable energies.

Kamarck told me the federal government purge of DEI programs has been largely effective, including overreaching efforts that impacted programs that studied breast cancer and ovarian cancer.

But Trump also used the power of the federal government to attack DEI programs at universities. Galston told me some universities just changed how they labeled some programs and job descriptions, as DEI has "gone into hiding" on campus.

Project 2025's aspirations to stamp out DEI programs, which the plan called "profoundly unserious," were a major focus for Trump's secretary of Defense, Pete Hegseth, even as America's military engaged in short-term hostilities with Venezuela and a prolonged war with Iran.

The result: Hegseth has forced out high-ranking officers or rejected their promotions, including several Black and female officers.

Hegseth wants to be called the "secretary of War." But he's too stuck on his worries about being "woke" to be much use in war.

Conservatives want big government. They just want to control it

For fossil fuels, Kamarck called the Trump administration's recent move to roll back mileage standards for new cars "was a biggie, and has been around for a while" on the list of conservative goals.

That also helps drive political division. "Over the past generation, energy has become more than an economic issue. It's become a cultural issue," Galston said. "Either you're for fossil fuels or you're against them."

Trump tried to control elections before. He's doing it again | Opinion

James Goodwin, a policy director at the Center for Progressive Reform, a nonprofit research organization, has tracked Project 2025's implementation and estimated that by February, about 53% of the plan had been initiated or enacted.

He found tension in the plan between the administrative-law overhaul envisioned when Project 2025 was written in 2023 and what happened when Trump took office and unleashed the federal government, people like Musk and his DOGE acolytes.

It can be difficult to track more Project 2025 progress, Goodwin said, as normal federal procedures are not followed, especially if the Republican-controlled Congress does little to provide oversight for implementation.

Goodwin cites the destruction of the U.S. Agency for International Development, a humanitarian program known as USAID, as a Project 2025 target that didn't go as Project 2025 projected. The plan had been to exert more presidential control over the agency, and to eliminate emphasis on DEI and climate change issues, while empowering "faith-based" organizations to run programs abroad.

"Instead, they just got rid of the whole thing," he told me, calling that "a trial balloon" for sweeping changes that upended how federal agencies are managed because Trump felt "zero pushback" to stop it.

Goodwin said that's not a problem for the Project 2025 authors because, in his opinion, this was never about the granular details of federal programs. Project 2025 moved on from the conservative ideal of a smaller government, shifting to a larger government as long as the people writing the plan hold the power.

"It was about a new way of thinking about government," Goodwin said. "It is a full-throated endorsement of a very specific kind of big government that is distinctly conservative."

Another view: Of course Trump lied about Project 2025. Now he's enacting it | Opinion

2026 midterms could be Project 2025's epilogue

Remember what Trump said during a 2024 presidential debate with Harris about Project 2025: "I have nothing to do with Project 2025. That's out there. I haven't read it. I don't want to read it, purposely. I'm not going to read it. This was a group of people that got together, they came up with some ideas. I guess some good, some bad. But it makes no difference." 

There are only two parts of that statement that sound remotely true – Trump didn't want to read the plan, and so he didn't. The rest is standard Trump distancing from terrible ideas he quickly embraced. It made a difference.

The 2026 midterm elections will determine if Republicans remain in control of Congress and continue to abet Trump's efforts to twist and transmogrify our federal government. The midterm polling shows a growing blue wave in support of Democrats winning control of Congress, which suggests Americans have seen enough of that.

That should be Project 2025's epilogue, and voters should keep that in mind when they cast their ballots.

Follow USA TODAY columnist Chris Brennan on Bluesky, @bychrisbrennan.bsky.social, and on X, @ByChrisBrennan. Sign up for his weekly newsletter, Translating Politics, here.

news.title: US Catholic voters weigh democracy, integrity as midterms approach
news.text:
"I think it's an abstract concept, and I think the people who may see the health of democracy as particularly salient are probably going to vote Democratic anyway," said Geoffrey Layman, chairman of the political science department at the University of Notre Dame. 

Layman noted that emphasizing democracy did not help President Joe Biden or Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election. But he said the issue may play differently amid corruption allegations in the federal government and billionaires seemingly profiting from their connections to power.

"I think that's closely related to democracy, but I think, especially when the economy is in a down period and people are struggling to make ends meet, I think that kind of corruption and profiteering off power sits particularly poorly with people," Layman told NCR.

Interviews with Catholic voters concerned about the future of democracy indicate they believe the executive branch under Trump has demonstrated autocratic tendencies and has gone unchecked by Congress and the courts. They also see an erosion of democratic norms and a weakening of the nation’s social fabric under Trump’s leadership.

"For me the biggest issue in the election is preserving the republic. Civil liberties have been ignored. The Constitution no longer protects us. There is no due process of law," said Gerald Ladouceur, a resident of Slingerlands, New York.

Ladoucer, 72, said the president is "a significant factor" in how he is voting. He said Trump "is trying to turn this country into a Christian nation, and as a Christian I am choosing candidates who are more inclusive of people from all faiths and no faith."

David Egan, 70, a Catholic deacon who lives outside Knoxville, Tennessee, told NCR that he sees the Trump administration as being contemptuous of constitutional checks on its power.

"I think that's probably the biggest issue, respecting the Constitution," Egan said.

Don Weigel, 72, a Catholic deacon in Buffalo, New York, had a similar view.

"Maybe the most important issue to me is electing a Congress, both the House and the Senate, that will be able to reign in the very autocratic tendencies that our president has," Weigel told NCR.
news.summary: A recent survey notes 73% of registered voters said the future of democracy was an important issue for them in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, second only to the economy.

news.title: The Morning Briefing: El-Sayed Gives Obama a Chance to Work Out His Trump Daddy Issues
news.text:
Top O' the Briefing

Happy Monday, dear Kruiser Morning Briefing friends. The Sine Qua Non Sequitur is spending the day judging a charcuterie haiku contest in one of the Dakotas.

Well, it's crunch time in this festive midterm election year. If we're lucky, things will be wrapped up by New Year's Eve, and we will know which direction the country is headed. news.title: "Large victory over Likud will ensure change": Gadi Eisenkot calls for support ahead of Israel election on Tuesday
news.text: Jerusalem [Israel], October 26 (ANI): Gadi Eisenkot the leader of Israel's Yashar party and a Prime Ministerial hopeful has called on citizens to vote in large numbers to ensure the defeat of incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday's elections to the Kneset.In a post on X, Eisenkot said, " In 24 hours, the fateful elections in the history of the state will begin, concerning its future, identity, and security. Yesterday we saw Netanyahu once again leaning on a campaign of intimidation, lies, and threats that included images of atomic bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv. This time it won't work for him. Donald Trump is a true friend of Israel. I appreciate his actions and commitment to Israel's security, and I am convinced that he will work in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people. Citizens of Israel, I believe in you that you will choose according to the dictates of your conscience and for the future of the State of Israel. Trust me. Straight! A large gap victory over the Likud will ensure the change and bring about the victory of the majority of the Zionist state-oriented camp in Israel."According to Jerusalem Post, the four latest election surveys, which closed on October 23, show that Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party leads Netanyahu's Likud, but neither of the two major political blocs has enough seats to secure a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.On Sunday, Netanyahu used the endorsement he got from US President Trump to project a doomsday scenario if his coalition does not come to power. Netanyahu posted an AI-generated image on social media depicting a nuclear explosion in Tel Aviv, warning the public just two days before the election that voting for anyone other than him could expose Israelis to the danger of a “second Holocaust.”Quoting Right-wing activist Yuval Blumberg's statements, Netanyahu's post read, “The State of Israel is in real and tangible existential danger. If the Iranians acquire nuclear weapons, nothing will ever be the same again. Everything is so trivial compared to the existential threat of Iran and the Shiite axis.""We have another two years of Trump to finish the work in Iran, and there's no telling what will come after that—whether it's Kamala Harris or some other mediocre figure. This is the window of time we have left to complete the necessary work to ensure our physical existence for the coming years. All the required resources of the state must be invested in this mission... This won't happen with a prime minister who can't pick up the phone and have a continuous, intimate conversation with Trump," the post read.Earlier, Trump endorsed Netanyahu for the second time saying, " When you go to the Polls, please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding Warrior Prime Minister! Israel was called The Little Satan, with the United States being called The Big Satan, by some very evil people. There can no longer be the chant heard around the World of “Death to America, Death to Israel,” and there won’t be. Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started." Israel uses a party-list proportional representation system. Under this system, voters cast their ballots for lists of candidates, and each list receives a number of seats in the Knesset proportional to its share of the vote. Israel has an electoral threshold: only lists that receive at least 3.25% of the valid votes participate in the allocation of Knesset seats. The Knesset is made up of 120 Members. (ANI)
